chapters.markdown:
The runoff result on the night of 30 October 2022 was close enough that the Superior Electoral Court called it only after 99.99 percent of the electronic ballot boxes had reported: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva 50.9 percent, Jair Bolsonaro 49.1 percent — a margin of just over two million votes in an electorate of 156 million. In the weeks before the vote, Bolsonaro had questioned the integrity of the voting machines so insistently that the court opened an inquiry into his conduct, and when the result came he did not concede. He stayed silent for nearly two days, and then gave a brief statement from the presidential palace in which he did not acknowledge defeat. The silence, the challenge to the returns, and the protest camps that formed outside army barracks afterward were not an aberration in a career that had otherwise respected institutional norms. They were a late expression of a style of politics that had been taking shape for thirty-five years.

The problem of judging a president like Jair Bolsonaro is that the evidence his supporters and his critics cite is often the same, and the disagreement is not only about the facts but about what counts as a fair measure of a leader. One side points to a pension reform that had eluded three previous presidents and says: he governed. The other side points to a pandemic that killed more than seven hundred thousand Brazilians and a president who called it a little flu and says: he failed his most basic duty. Both claims are anchored in the record, and neither can be reduced to a mistake about the data. To weigh them together is to ask how a president’s appeal to the people who put him in office relates to what his government actually did, and to ask it over the whole arc of a public life that began long before the Planalto Palace.

The arc began inside an institution whose discipline he would invoke for the rest of his career but whose rules he repeatedly tested. Jair Messias Bolsonaro was born in Glicério, a small municipality in the interior of São Paulo, on 21 March 1955, and grew up in Eldorado, in the Ribeira Valley. He entered the Preparatory School of the Brazilian Army in 1973 and graduated from the Agulhas Negras Military Academy as an artillery officer in 1977. For the next decade he served in field artillery units in Mato Grosso do Sul and Rio de Janeiro, reaching the rank of captain. Nothing in that record distinguished him from hundreds of other officers until 1986, when he wrote an article for *Veja* magazine that criticized the military’s pay scales and argued that the officer corps was being treated unfairly. The army hierarchy condemned the article, and Bolsonaro spent fifteen days in detention for insubordination. Among fellow officers and their families, however, the gesture was celebrated. A political identity had been forged: the captain who spoke out, the man who said what others in uniform only muttered.

A year later that identity was tested far more severely. In October 1987 *Veja* reported that Bolsonaro had drawn up plans to detonate explosives at military installations in Rio de Janeiro — barracks, a water tower, an oil pipeline — as a protest against low wages. The allegation was not a rumor passed among journalists; it was investigated by the army, and Bolsonaro was court-martialed. The case turned on two kinds of evidence. The first was the testimony of fellow officers, some of whom said Bolsonaro had sketched the plan on a napkin during a conversation. The second was a set of graphological exams meant to link his handwriting to diagrams found in the investigation. The Supreme Military Court, the highest tribunal in the military justice system, heard the case in 1988 and acquitted him. The reporting general who reviewed the evidence recommended acquittal, citing contradictory witness statements and unreliable handwriting analysis. On that basis, the court found the charges unproven, and Bolsonaro left active service in December 1988, entering the army reserve with the rank of captain.

The acquittal is the legal fact, and it is the fact Bolsonaro has relied on ever since. But it is not the only fact in the record. In 2018, as Bolsonaro campaigned for the presidency, official documents from the army’s own administrative review came to light. That review, conducted inside the military bureaucracy and separate from the criminal court-martial, had reached a different conclusion. The administrative body found Bolsonaro guilty unanimously. Its written assessment described a “serious personality deviation,” a “professional deformation,” and a lack of moral courage to leave the Army, and it stated that he had “lied throughout the process.” The language is bureaucratic, but its severity is unmistakable. The institution that Bolsonaro would later hold up as the model of order and patriotism had, in its internal judgment, deemed him unfit.

Two things can be true at once, and they are. The criminal proceeding ended in acquittal on grounds that a court of law considered sufficient. The administrative proceeding produced a finding of guilt that the army’s own officers endorsed. Neither document is a conspiracy, and neither is a complete portrait. What they establish together is that Bolsonaro’s departure from the military was not a clean severance but a rupture that left behind two incompatible official accounts. The man who entered electoral politics in 1989 carried with him the persona of the outspoken captain, the martyr of the pay dispute, and the unresolved controversy of the bomb plot. His supporters would see a persecuted truth-teller; his critics would see a man who had been caught and let go. The ambiguity was never fully settled, and it would prove remarkably durable.

Bolsonaro’s first elected office was a seat on the Rio de Janeiro city council, which he won in 1988 for the Christian Democratic Party and held for barely two years. The council was a way station, not a career. In 1990 he ran for the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Brazil’s National Congress, and won a seat representing Rio de Janeiro. He would hold that seat for seven consecutive terms, twenty-seven years in the same chamber, before ascending to the presidency. The longevity alone is a fact that resists easy caricature. Whatever else Bolsonaro was, he was a professional politician who survived repeated elections across three decades, and the voters of Rio de Janeiro returned him to office again and again.

The congressional career that followed was built on a narrow but stable set of themes. Bolsonaro spoke for military families and police officers, for the retired and the enlisted, and he did so in a voice that was deliberately unpolished. He defended the 1964–1985 military dictatorship openly and often. He opposed abortion, same-sex marriage, and what he called “gender ideology.” He called for looser gun laws and harsher criminal penalties. In a legislature where most members shifted their rhetoric to match the coalition of the moment, Bolsonaro’s positions remained fixed, and his manner of expressing them — blunt, confrontational, frequently insulting — became his signature. He was not a legislator who built majorities or chaired influential committees. Of the dozens of bills he introduced, only a handful became law. His power lay elsewhere: in the attention he commanded, the loyalty he cultivated among a specific constituency, and the immunity his provocations seemed to grant him from the normal costs of political combat.

The party labels under which he served tell their own story. He moved from the Christian Democratic Party to the Reform Progressive Party, then to the Brazilian Progressive Party, the Brazilian Labour Party, the Liberal Front Party, the Progressive Party again, the Social Christian Party, and finally, in 2018, the Social Liberal Party. Eight parties in twenty-seven years. The constant switching was not ideological drift — his positions barely moved — but a search for vehicles that would nominate him without constraining him. Each party gave him a ballot line; none gave him a power base inside the organization. He was a party of one, and his durability came from the direct relationship he maintained with his voters, a relationship that television and, later, social media amplified far beyond what his legislative output would have justified.

In 1993, two years into his second term in the Chamber, Bolsonaro gave an interview to the news magazine *Veja* that distilled his politics into a single exchange. Asked about the military regime, he said that its great mistake had been to torture rather than to kill. The remark was not an aside. It was a deliberate provocation, and it was followed, in the same period, by speeches on the floor of the Chamber in which he argued that a return to military rule was the only way to rescue Brazil from corruption and disorder. The dictatorship, in his telling, had been a period of stability and economic growth cut short by weakness and subversion. The democratic governments that followed had squandered that inheritance.

The mechanism by which these statements operated was straightforward, and it reveals something about the political ecosystem Bolsonaro was learning to navigate. A deputy says something that would end most careers. The press reports it. The political class condemns it. The deputy’s core supporters — military families, conservative Catholics, voters who remembered the dictatorship as a time of order — hear it not as a scandal but as a confirmation. The condemnation from elites becomes evidence of the deputy’s authenticity. The cycle repeats, and each repetition widens the gap between the deputy’s reputation inside the chamber and his reputation among a slice of the public. By the mid-1990s, Bolsonaro had mastered this cycle. He was a marginal figure in the Congress and a known figure in the country, and the two facts were not contradictory. They were causally connected.

The political ground that would eventually make a Bolsonaro presidency conceivable began to shift long after he had settled into his role as a congressional provocateur. The shift was not the work of any single event but of a cascade that started with the massive street protests of June 2013, continued through the unraveling of the Workers’ Party’s governing project, and accelerated with the lava jato corruption investigation that began to devour the political class in 2014. The protests had begun over a bus-fare increase in São Paulo and had swollen into a diffuse national revolt against the cost and quality of public services, the privileges of politicians, and the impunity of the powerful. No party channeled that energy, and no leader captured it. The protests were a symptom of a system under strain, not a movement with a program.

The strain became a fracture in 2014, when the Federal Police launched Operation Car Wash, a corruption investigation centered on the state oil company Petrobras that would eventually implicate executives, politicians, and parties across the spectrum. The investigation revealed a system of kickbacks and campaign financing so extensive that it touched the presidencies of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Dilma Rousseff, the leadership of the Workers’ Party, and senior figures in the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party, the Progressive Party, and others. The political establishment did not merely lose credibility; it was indicted, arrested, and convicted in real time, on television, over a period of years. Voters who had once divided along partisan lines began to coalesce around a simpler distinction: the corrupt and the clean.

Rousseff’s impeachment in 2016 was the institutional expression of that collapse. The formal charge was fiscal mismanagement — the use of accounting maneuvers to disguise the size of the budget deficit — but the political force behind it was the broader delegitimization of the Workers’ Party’s thirteen-year hold on the presidency. The impeachment removed Rousseff and installed her vice president, Michel Temer, whose own government would soon be tainted by corruption allegations. By the time the 2018 presidential campaign began, the two parties that had dominated Brazilian politics since the return to democracy — the Workers’ Party and the Brazilian Social Democracy Party — were both discredited, and the space for an outsider had opened wide.

[Figure: How political crisis and party disillusionment created openings for a new candidacy]

The opening was not empty. It was filled by several distinct currents that Bolsonaro’s candidacy would eventually draw together, and listing them is a way of seeing that his rise was less a personal conquest than an alignment of forces that had been building for years. The first current was anti-corruption sentiment, the conviction, hardened by Car Wash, that the political system was a criminal enterprise and that only someone outside it could be trusted. Bolsonaro had spent twenty-seven years in the Chamber of Deputies, but he had never been a minister, never led a major party, and never been implicated in the Petrobras scandals. His very marginality became a credential.

The second current was conservative social politics. Brazil had undergone rapid cultural change in the preceding two decades: the legal recognition of same-sex unions, the expansion of abortion rights in limited circumstances, the growing visibility of feminist and LGBTQ movements, and a series of Supreme Federal Court decisions that social conservatives viewed as judicial overreach. A large and organized constituency — evangelical Protestants, traditionalist Catholics, and voters who felt alienated from urban secular culture — was looking for a champion. Bolsonaro, a professed Catholic who had been baptized in the Jordan River by an evangelical pastor during a 2016 trip to Israel, spoke their language without hedging.

The third current was dissatisfaction with conventional parties. The Workers’ Party, even in defeat, retained a loyal base, but it also provoked intense rejection among voters who blamed it for the recession, the corruption, and the crime wave that had pushed Brazil’s homicide rate above sixty thousand a year. The Brazilian Social Democracy Party, the main center-left alternative, had been hollowed out by its alliance with Temer and its own corruption scandals. Smaller parties were patronage machines with little ideological coherence. Millions of voters wanted none of them, and Bolsonaro’s party-hopping biography, which had once marked him as a political vagrant, now read as proof that he had never been co-opted.

The claim that Bolsonaro’s rise followed chiefly from his personal appeal has a surface plausibility. He was, by any measure, a compelling figure on a stage full of gray men. His manner was direct, his language was unvarnished, and his willingness to say things that others would not — about crime, about the dictatorship, about his political opponents — gave his rallies the feel of a release rather than a persuasion. The knife attack in Juiz de Fora on 6 September 2018, when a mentally disturbed man stabbed him in the abdomen during a campaign event, turned him into a martyr and a patient, and it removed him from the televised debates where his vulnerabilities might have been exposed. His sons, especially Flávio and Eduardo, built parallel political careers that amplified his message. The personal story is real, and it matters.

But a personal story is not the same as a personal cause. The conditions that made Bolsonaro’s candidacy viable were structural before they were biographical. The impeachment of a president, the criminal prosecution of a generation of political leaders, a recession that had thrown thirteen million people out of work, and a homicide epidemic that had made public safety the overwhelming concern of ordinary Brazilians — these were not created by one man’s charisma. They were the accumulated failures of a political system that had promised growth, stability, and inclusion and had delivered stagnation, scandal, and fear. Bolsonaro did not manufacture the demand for an outsider. He stepped into a demand that already existed and gave it a voice.

The voice was recognizable because it had been audible, in one form or another, for decades. The captain who had been court-martialed in 1988, the deputy who had praised the dictatorship in 1993, the congressman who had switched parties eight times while never moderating his positions — this was not a figure invented for the 2018 campaign. It was a figure who had been built, patiently and publicly, over a long career, and who had accumulated a constituency that knew exactly what it was getting. The retrospective temptation is to treat that career as a prelude, a series of hints that only become legible once the presidency is in view. But the career was not a prelude. It was the thing itself, and the presidency, when it came, was an extension of its logic rather than a break from it.

What the pre-presidential record establishes is not that Bolsonaro was destined for power, nor that his eventual coalition was the only possible outcome of the forces that gathered in the 2010s. Other outsiders could have filled the space. Other messages could have organized the discontent. The record establishes something narrower and more useful: that Bolsonaro, by the time he became a serious presidential candidate, was a known quantity. His admirers and his detractors both had ample evidence for their assessments, and neither side had to guess. The question the presidency would answer was not who Jair Bolsonaro was. It was what a man like that would do with the powers the constitution gave him, and whether the institutions that had contained him as a deputy could contain him as a president.

chapters.markdown:
Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the abdomen on the afternoon of September 6, 2018, during a campaign event in Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais. He was rushed to a local hospital and underwent emergency surgery. The operation controlled internal bleeding from five wounds: one in the mesenteric artery, one in the large intestine and three in the small intestine. Doctors performed a colostomy. Bolsonaro, 63, was stable in intensive care but remained at risk and could not yet be transferred; his recovery was expected to take three to four weeks.

Adélio Bispo de Oliveira, 40, was identified as the attacker and arrested at the scene. He told police he had stabbed Bolsonaro for personal reasons and in the name of God.

Authorities and other presidential hopefuls reacted immediately, including Bolsonaro’s fiercest rivals.

The registered plan titled *O Caminho da Prosperidade* offered a formal outline of what Jair Bolsonaro said he would do in government. It was a compact document, less a detailed program for administration than a set of commitments arranged under broad headings: security, economic freedom, social questions, and a state presented as burdened by corruption and inefficiency. Its title, “The Path to Prosperity,” made a national promise. The text’s political work was to give that promise a recognizable direction without requiring every supporter to agree on the route.

On security, the plan joined public order to the rights of citizens and the freedom to defend themselves. Bolsonaro’s campaign statements sharpened that language. He advocated loosening restrictions on gun ownership and giving police greater latitude in confronting suspected criminals. He also spoke of deploying the military against crime. The proposals addressed a country where homicide and robbery were not abstractions, and where many voters saw the state as failing to protect them. But they did not amount to a single operational blueprint. The platform named a posture; the campaign’s sharper declarations supplied its force.

The economic pages made a different appeal. They promised privatization, lower barriers to enterprise, and a reduction in the reach of the state. Paulo Guedes, the economist who became the campaign’s principal economic adviser, gave these commitments a market-oriented vocabulary. To business audiences and voters who blamed public spending and political patronage for stagnation, the language suggested a break with the economic policies associated with the Workers’ Party. Yet the plan did not settle every question about how quickly privatization would proceed, which state companies would be sold, or how the costs of adjustment would be distributed. Its clarity lay in direction, not in a complete map.

The social language was more categorical. Bolsonaro opposed abortion and same-sex marriage and invoked the traditional family as a national value. That position could be heard as a promise to defend religious conviction against a cultural elite believed to be indifferent or hostile to it. It also reached beyond church membership: voters who did not identify as evangelical could share opposition to the Workers’ Party, support for conservative social norms, or distrust of rapid cultural change. The plan’s vocabulary bundled those concerns together, while the people who responded to it did not necessarily hold them in equal measure.

Its anti-corruption promise carried an especially strong political charge. The campaign presented Bolsonaro as clean in contrast with a political class discredited by the Lava Jato investigations and the scandals surrounding established parties. He supported the proposed Ten Measures Against Corruption and spoke as though personal distance from the old political order could itself guarantee a different kind of government. The claim was persuasive as a contrast, but a presidential program required more than the candidate’s self-presentation: it required rules, appointments, legislative partners, and a willingness to accept constraints. The plan named the desired virtue more plainly than it described the work of making it durable.

That gap did not make the platform meaningless. A government plan filed with the TSE was a public commitment, and its language mattered. It told voters which concerns Bolsonaro’s campaign would elevate and which kinds of change it would call legitimate. But it cannot be read as a transcript of the coalition’s collective wishes. An evangelical voter might have placed family policy first; a police officer, public security; an investor, privatization; an anti-PT voter, the defeat of a party associated with corruption. Many could support the same candidate for different reasons, and some could disagree with parts of the plan while treating the election as a choice between political camps.

The document’s broadness was therefore both a limitation and a political asset. It left unresolved questions that would become consequential in office, but it allowed a coalition to assemble around direction, identity, and opposition before its members had to agree on administrative detail. Bolsonaro’s campaign offered a common adversary and a set of signals. It did not offer one common account of what prosperity, order, or family protection would require in every policy area.

The signals were repeated in different registers, each aimed at a constituency that could recognize its own grievance without being asked to share every other voter’s priorities. Public security came first in the campaign’s emotional vocabulary. Bolsonaro promised easier access to guns, stronger police powers, and a more forceful response to crime. Men were particularly receptive to his security appeal, but fear of violence was not confined to male voters, nor did support for tougher policing imply agreement on every proposal. For many, the promise began with a simple judgment: the state had not kept people safe.

Corruption supplied a second signal. Bolsonaro attacked the established parties and associated the Workers’ Party with the scandals exposed during Lava Jato. He presented himself as an incorruptible outsider, though he had spent decades in Congress. The appeal depended less on absence from politics than on a claim to stand outside the political class that voters blamed. Anti-PT voters could hear in it a promise to punish a party they opposed; others heard a general demand for cleaner government.

Social conservatism addressed evangelical Christians and a wider public uneasy with changes in family and gender politics. Opposition to abortion and same-sex marriage, alongside the language of faith and traditional family, made the campaign legible to religious voters who wanted their moral commitments represented in national politics. Evangelical communities were not a single bloc, however. Pastors, congregations, and individual voters differed in their political judgments, and religious identity did not dictate a vote.

National identity gave these messages a shared frame. Bolsonaro’s military background and praise for order offered some voters a language of patriotism, discipline, and national restoration. The same symbols unsettled others, especially those who associated military rule with repression. His running mate, General Hamilton Mourão, reinforced the campaign’s military associations, while Bolsonaro’s opponents argued that his rhetoric threatened democratic norms.

The economic message completed the inventory without resolving its tensions. Privatization and a smaller state appealed to business interests and voters who favored market reform; the promise of security and state force appealed to voters who wanted government to act more aggressively. Those positions could coexist in a campaign because they answered different frustrations. Their compatibility in governing would be harder to assume.

The campaign did not need every supporter to share one theory of Brazil’s problems. It needed each group to recognize a reason to vote for the same candidate, and a reason to believe that the alternative was worse.

The communication system helped make that coalition visible to itself. Bolsonaro used social media and messaging applications, especially WhatsApp, to circulate statements directly to supporters and to encourage their further distribution. The candidate could appear without the filtering conventions of a press conference or a newspaper interview. A short video, a forwarded message, or a post could carry a political identity as much as a policy proposal: the speaker was not merely making a claim but refusing the manners and gatekeeping associated with established media.

That directness strengthened the anti-establishment appeal, but it did not mean conventional news coverage had become irrelevant. Newspapers and television continued to report the campaign, scrutinize its statements, and provide a common arena in which candidates could be compared. Bolsonaro’s attacks on the press could themselves become news, giving his conflict with journalists a second life beyond the original exchange. Coverage that criticized him might reach voters who saw it as evidence of bias; coverage that repeated his claims might extend their reach. The old and new channels were not separate systems. They fed one another.

The campaign’s advantage was not simply that social media bypassed editors. It was that the candidate’s public style fit a medium in which sharp conflict traveled easily. A direct accusation against the political class could be clipped and shared; a conventional interview could be recast as proof that the press was hostile. Supporters did not need to accept every claim to value the posture. The communication offered recognition: the candidate spoke as though he were addressing people whom established politicians had ignored and established journalists misunderstood.

This pattern had limits. WhatsApp groups were not a reliable census of the electorate, and the circulation of a message did not prove that every recipient believed it. The campaign’s reach also depended on older political networks, religious communities, family ties, and the news attention that helped make Bolsonaro a national figure. Digital communication could accelerate and personalize the campaign, but it could not by itself explain why the messages resonated. The recession, corruption scandals, insecurity, and hostility to the Workers’ Party gave them an audience.

Nor did direct communication necessarily produce a shared program. A voter receiving a message about guns might support Bolsonaro for security while knowing little about privatization; a business supporter might welcome Guedes while disliking the candidate’s social rhetoric. The same channel could bind people to a leader while leaving their policy priorities distinct. That combination—personal identification without full agreement—was central to the coalition’s strength and would later complicate claims that the result endorsed every promise equally.

After the attack in Juiz de Fora, the campaign changed its form. Bolsonaro could no longer conduct the ordinary sequence of public rallies and face-to-face appearances on which a candidate might rely. His recovery and hospitalization narrowed his physical campaign, while his supporters and advisers continued to circulate his message. The interruption did not erase the campaign’s existing networks; it made the candidate’s absence from public events part of the immediate political landscape.

The first round on October 7 placed Bolsonaro ahead of Fernando Haddad, the Workers’ Party candidate, with 46.03 percent of valid votes to Haddad’s 29.28 percent. The result established that Bolsonaro had entered the runoff with a substantial lead, not that the election was settled. The second round required him to attract voters whose first choices had been eliminated, including people who had supported other conservative candidates and those whose principal aim was to prevent a Workers’ Party return.

His reduced public schedule also changed the balance between the candidate’s own appearances and mediated communication. Supporters could share messages and images without waiting for a rally; television coverage continued to frame the contest for viewers who were not members of campaign networks. The campaign’s direct style had already made Bolsonaro a familiar figure. The period after Juiz de Fora tested whether that familiarity could sustain a national candidacy when the candidate could not campaign in the usual way.

The immediate political consequence was not a single conversion of sympathy into votes. The attack intensified attention, but Bolsonaro’s support had been built before it, through security, anti-corruption, social conservatism, and rejection of the Workers’ Party. Treating the event as the cause of his victory would erase those earlier alignments; treating it as irrelevant would ignore how abruptly it altered the campaign’s public rhythm. The runoff was won through a coalition that existed before the interruption and continued to operate through channels that did not depend on the candidate’s physical presence.

The coalition’s components were related, but they were not interchangeable. Evangelical voters formed one important source of support, and Bolsonaro’s opposition to abortion and same-sex marriage gave many a clear reason to prefer him. Religious leaders could help make political choices visible within congregations, but evangelical voters were not a uniform electorate. Their concerns included family policy and religious liberty, while their judgments about economic policy, poverty, and democratic conduct could differ. The campaign’s religious language opened a door; it did not determine every vote that crossed it.

Security constituencies responded to a different promise. Police officers, military personnel, and voters anxious about crime could value Bolsonaro’s pledge to expand gun access and give law enforcement greater freedom. His own military background reinforced that appeal. Yet the category included people with varied views of policing, the armed forces, and the proper limits of state power. A voter who wanted more effective protection did not necessarily endorse every proposal made in the name of security.

Business interests had another basis for support. Guedes’s presence and the promise of privatization suggested a government more favorable to markets and less committed to state-led economic management. For investors and business leaders, this could outweigh discomfort with Bolsonaro’s social rhetoric or his confrontational style. But business was not a single constituency, and support for economic liberalization did not mean every firm or executive agreed on the pace and scope of reform.

Anti-Workers’ Party voters were the broadest and least programmatically specific group. Some opposed the party because of corruption scandals; others rejected its economic record or its social and political agenda. Still others treated the election as a choice between two camps and voted against the Workers’ Party without strong attachment to Bolsonaro. Their negative preference could help create a majority, but it could not tell a president what those voters would support once the common opponent disappeared.

These groups overlapped. An evangelical voter might also be a police officer; a business owner might be motivated chiefly by opposition to the Workers’ Party. Their overlap helped the campaign present a coherent public image, but the reasons for support remained plural. The coalition was strongest as an electoral alliance, where a vote for one candidate could express several different judgments at once. Its unity was less certain as a governing mandate, where those judgments would have to be translated into choices among competing policies.

The case for calling Bolsonaro’s victory a coherent popular mandate deserves to be stated plainly. He finished first in the initial round and won the runoff by a clear margin. He campaigned openly on public security, economic liberalization, social conservatism, and opposition to the Workers’ Party. Voters had access to his public statements and knew that he rejected the political style of the established parties. A democratic result cannot be dismissed because the winning coalition contained different kinds of voters. If a candidate wins under the rules, he has a legitimate claim to govern.

That claim is strongest when it refers to the authority to take office and pursue the commitments made in the campaign. It is weaker when expanded into an assertion that the electorate endorsed every proposal, or that one interpretation of the victory can speak for all supporters. The official result counts votes for candidates, not reasons for voting. It cannot tell us whether a person chose Bolsonaro because of guns, family policy, privatization, anti-corruption, or opposition to the Workers’ Party. Nor does a winning margin turn a campaign promise into a detailed public instruction on how to implement it.

The formal platform makes the difficulty visible. *O Caminho da Prosperidade* offered broad directions, while campaign statements sometimes made those directions more forceful and specific. Voters could support the promise of order without endorsing every measure proposed in its name. They could favor economic reform without agreeing that every state company should be privatized. They could reject the Workers’ Party without treating Bolsonaro’s personal claims as proof of incorruptibility. Electoral support joined these positions for the purpose of choosing a president; it did not erase their differences.

The mandate argument also risks confusing popularity with administrative consent. A president may claim authority from a majority and still face a Congress elected on its own terms, courts charged with enforcing constitutional limits, and state governments with responsibilities of their own. The campaign’s anti-establishment language could make such constraints appear to supporters as obstruction, but the election did not abolish them. Winning office gives a president power to govern within the constitutional system, not a blank authorization to redefine its boundaries.

The fairest judgment is therefore neither that the victory meant nothing beyond a temporary protest nor that it expressed a single national program. Bolsonaro’s win was a genuine democratic mandate to hold the presidency and pursue the broad direction he had advertised. It was not evidence that every voter shared his priorities, accepted every campaign statement, or consented in advance to every governing choice. The distinction is especially important because his coalition had been assembled through messages that were complementary in an election but potentially in tension in office.

The official runoff returns make the scale of the victory concrete while also showing its geography. The TSE counted 57,797,847 votes for Jair Bolsonaro and 47,040,906 for Fernando Haddad on October 28, 2018. Bolsonaro carried the national contest, but the distribution was not uniform: Haddad’s strongest support lay in much of the Northeast, while Bolsonaro prevailed across much of the South, Southeast, and Center-West. The figure presents the national totals alongside selected regional shares, so the margin can be read against the map of the electorate rather than as a single undifferentiated number.

[Figure: 2018 presidential runoff: votes and regional vote shares]

The figure’s national totals describe a decisive result, while its regional shares resist the idea of a single, evenly distributed political conversion. Bolsonaro’s support was broad enough to win, but it was stronger in some regions than others, and the pattern reflected differences in political histories, economic interests, and local alignments. A national majority can be real without being socially uniform.

That is why the result should be read as both a mandate and a coalition. It authorized Bolsonaro to govern, and it showed that his campaign had brought together voters who had not previously needed to agree on a common program. The returns tell us who prevailed and by how much; they do not settle what each voter intended. Those intentions must be inferred cautiously from the campaign’s messages and the constituencies that answered them, not assigned wholesale to the winner as a single national will.

The administration Bolsonaro brought to office was not a cabinet in which one professional language prevailed. It joined military officers, elected politicians, economists, prosecutors, diplomats, and specialists whose authority came from different places and whose expectations of the presidency did not necessarily coincide. The initial cabinet had twenty-two ministries, down from twenty-nine under Michel Temer. Seven ministers were identified as military figures, eight as technocrats, and seven as politicians, categories that overlapped in practice and did not describe every appointment neatly. Two women entered the initial cabinet; no Black Brazilian did. The composition was a statement about whom Bolsonaro trusted and what kinds of standing he wanted around him, but it was also a working arrangement that would have to hold together through disputes over policy and control.

Paulo Guedes, the economist placed at the head of a newly enlarged Economy Ministry, represented the promise of market-oriented reform. His appointment gathered finance, planning, industry, and other economic functions under one roof, giving him a broad brief and a prominent place in the government’s public account of itself. The pension reform that Congress eventually approved was consequential, but the ministry’s reach did not make the president a consistent advocate of every measure Guedes favored. Bolsonaro could endorse fiscal restraint and then resist politically costly changes; Guedes could be central to the government’s economic program without controlling its political priorities. The relationship made the cabinet’s technocratic element visible, and exposed its limits.

Military officers occupied a different kind of space. General Fernando Azevedo e Silva became defense minister, the first serving or former military officer to hold the post since the ministry was created in 1999. Other current or former officers led ministries including Health, Infrastructure, Science and Technology, and Mining and Energy at different points. By the end of 2020, military personnel had become a substantial presence in civilian government, extending well beyond the cabinet. That presence carried the prestige and administrative experience Bolsonaro associated with the armed forces, while also raising questions about the boundary between military and civilian roles. A minister’s uniformed background did not make every decision a military decision; the accumulation of appointments nevertheless altered the government’s character and the public’s perception of who stood behind it.

The civilian political figures had their own sources of leverage. Onyx Lorenzoni, a long-serving deputy, became chief of staff, while Tereza Cristina brought experience in agricultural politics to the Agriculture Ministry. Sergio Moro arrived from the judiciary with public standing built through anti-corruption prosecutions and took the Justice and Public Security portfolio. These appointments were not interchangeable. Moro’s reputation depended on a claim to legal independence; a congressional politician’s influence depended on negotiation; a military minister might be valued for discipline and command. Bolsonaro’s administration placed all of these forms of authority close to the presidency, but did not establish a common method for reconciling them.

The arrangement could produce real policy work. Guedes’s team pursued economic changes; Moro’s ministry combined public security and justice; ministers with military backgrounds brought experience in large organizations. Yet the president’s own style made loyalty and public alignment unusually important. Ministers were not merely expected to administer their portfolios. They were also drawn into a political language organized around Bolsonaro’s declared causes, his enemies, and his direct exchanges with supporters. In the April 2020 meeting, he spoke of changing security personnel and, if necessary, the minister; he also treated favorable coverage of a minister as grounds for suspicion. That was a revealing account of the presidency’s internal logic: formal responsibility mattered, but so did the president’s personal judgment of who was serving him.

A cabinet can contain different kinds of expertise and still work coherently when disagreements are settled through clear procedures and ministers can defend decisions without treating every dispute as a test of allegiance. Bolsonaro’s cabinet had no shortage of prominent figures. Its difficulty was that their standing often rested on separate constituencies and separate claims to authority, while the president’s communications made conflict a recurring way of defining political loyalty. The result was not a single military or technocratic government. It was a shifting coalition inside the executive, held together in part by access to Bolsonaro and repeatedly tested by his demands.

The changing roster gives that instability a chronology. The figure traces ministerial departures from 2019 through 2022, using appointment and dismissal dates checked against cabinet chronologies. It shows the timing and frequency of exits across the term.

[Figure: Ministerial departures during Bolsonaro’s presidency]

The first year brought departures as the new government settled into office. Gustavo Bebianno, who had managed Bolsonaro’s campaign and became chief of staff, left in February 2019 after a public dispute involving the president’s son Carlos Bolsonaro and allegations about campaign financing. Ricardo Vélez Rodríguez, the education minister, was dismissed in April after months of internal conflict and criticism of his management. In June, Santos Cruz, a retired general serving as chief of the Government Secretariat, was removed after a dispute over the influence of the president’s sons and the government’s communication operation. Each case involved a different portfolio and immediate cause; together they showed that seniority and military credentials did not guarantee tenure when a minister became entangled in a conflict close to the president.

The following year brought a more consequential rupture. Moro resigned in April, and Nelson Teich left the Health Ministry in May, less than a month after taking office, amid disagreement over the federal response to COVID-19. In June, Abraham Weintraub left Education for a post at the World Bank after repeated attacks on the Supreme Federal Court. The departures did not all arise from the same conflict, but their timing placed the government’s handling of the pandemic and its relations with the courts at the center of cabinet instability. In 2021, Ernesto Araújo left Foreign Affairs after criticism of his diplomacy and the government’s vaccine procurement; Ricardo Salles departed Environment in June as the Supreme Federal Court authorized an investigation into alleged irregularities in timber exports. The year also saw the replacement of Defense Minister Fernando Azevedo e Silva, followed by the resignations of the commanders of the Army, Navy, and Air Force.

The final year was shaped by the election calendar and a larger wave of departures as ministers left to run for office. The figure’s annual counts do not distinguish a minister forced out after a dispute from one who departed to pursue a candidacy, and that difference matters. Turnover can register conflict, ordinary political rotation, or both. But the sequence from Bebianno to Moro, from Teich to Azevedo e Silva, shows that the cabinet’s instability was not confined to one faction or one policy. It repeatedly reached posts whose work required sustained coordination: the presidency’s political office, health, justice, defense, education, and foreign affairs.

Moro’s resignation made the problem of presidential control unusually explicit. On April 24, 2020, the former judge appeared on television and announced that he was leaving the Justice and Public Security Ministry. The immediate issue was Bolsonaro’s decision to remove Maurício Valeixo as director-general of the Federal Police. Valeixo had been appointed during Moro’s tenure, and Moro said he had not been consulted about the dismissal. The police director’s post mattered because the Federal Police investigated federal crimes and could conduct inquiries involving people close to the government. Moro’s objection was not simply that a minister had lost a personnel dispute. He alleged that Bolsonaro wanted influence over the police leadership for reasons connected to investigations.

The sequence had begun the previous day, when the government published Valeixo’s dismissal in the Official Gazette. The notice presented the departure as occurring at the director’s request and bore Bolsonaro’s signature alongside Valeixo’s. Moro disputed that account, saying Valeixo had not asked to leave and that he had not agreed to the wording. Bolsonaro later said he had the power to choose the police chief and wanted a director with whom he could communicate. That authority was not in dispute in the abstract: the president appointed the director-general. The conflict concerned the purpose of the appointment and whether the president was seeking access to investigations or information that should remain insulated from personal political use.

In his televised statement, Moro described a pattern of pressure. He said Bolsonaro had repeatedly asked for information about the Federal Police and had complained that he could not obtain reports from the Rio de Janeiro office. Moro connected the effort to replace Valeixo with the president’s interest in changing leadership in Rio, where investigations included matters involving Bolsonaro’s family. The allegations were grave, but they were not proven simply by the resignation. They prompted an investigation authorized by Supreme Federal Court Justice Celso de Mello, who assigned Federal Police investigators to examine the claims. Bolsonaro denied wrongdoing and argued that a president had legitimate reasons to seek a direct line to the agency responsible for public security.

The institutional process had several steps. Moro’s public accusation was referred to the Supreme Federal Court; the court authorized an inquiry; investigators collected testimony and records; and the attorney general’s office would have to decide whether the evidence warranted a criminal charge. In May, the court released the recording of the April 22 ministerial meeting, which Moro had identified as relevant. The recording showed Bolsonaro speaking of changing security personnel and, if he could not replace someone directly, changing the minister responsible. It also showed him linking the matter to his family and friends. Those statements gave investigators material to assess, but they did not by themselves establish that he had interfered in a particular criminal investigation.

Moro’s departure therefore exposed a conflict between two claims of executive power. A president must be able to appoint senior officials and receive information needed to govern. A justice minister, however, is responsible for protecting the independence of law enforcement from partisan use. The official inquiry tested whether Bolsonaro had crossed that line; the resignation made visible how quickly a dispute over an appointment could become a public contest over the integrity of the state. Moro’s allegation remained an allegation, not a judicial finding. The episode still demonstrated the cost of a governing relationship in which a minister’s disagreement with the president could not be contained within the cabinet.

The meeting that Moro pointed to is valuable because it records more than a dispute about the Federal Police. Its nearly two hours place Bolsonaro among ministers in the Palácio do Planalto on April 22, 2020, as Brazil was confronting the first months of the pandemic. The released audiovisual record is a primary source for how the president addressed his cabinet, but it is not a complete account of every private exchange in the government or a transcript of every decision made. Its force lies in the words and relations it captures: the president’s expectations, the ministers’ interventions, and the way policy and loyalty became entangled in one meeting.

Bolsonaro’s remarks on security are direct. He says he cannot wait for his family and friends to be harmed, complains that he has been unable to change security personnel in Rio de Janeiro, and describes a chain of replacements that could reach the minister. The passage matters because the chain is concrete: a person at the operational end, that person’s superior, and finally the minister. It presents the president’s frustration as a problem of command and access. Moro’s later account gave the exchange a specific interpretation, connecting it to the Federal Police and investigations. The recording supports the fact that Bolsonaro pressed for changes in security personnel and invoked his family; it does not, without additional evidence, settle the purpose of every requested change.

The wider meeting is less orderly than a formal cabinet presentation. Paulo Guedes argues for privatizing Banco do Brasil. Abraham Weintraub attacks the Supreme Federal Court and says he would put its members in prison. Damares Alves discusses a court ruling on abortion. The comments occur amid an emergency that had placed the Health Ministry at the center of national attention, yet the minister’s voice is limited in the recording. The meeting’s tone is not merely coarse. It shifts repeatedly from policy to denunciation, from administrative questions to accusations against judges, journalists, governors, and political opponents. The president’s language sets a pattern in which the cabinet can speak as a political camp under attack, rather than as a group of officials responsible for distinct public functions.

Bolsonaro’s remarks about the pandemic sharpen that pattern. He calls the governors of São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro abusive names, criticizes the mayor of Manaus, and frames the dispute over restrictions as a struggle over liberty. He says that freedom is more important than life, a statement that joined a political principle to a public-health crisis in the most provocative possible form. The recording does not tell us how every listener understood the sentence. It does show that the president’s argument about restrictions was not presented as a technical disagreement over the balance of health risks, economic costs, and legal powers. It was cast as a confrontation between freedom and those he accused of exploiting the virus.

The meeting also contains an account of political belonging. Bolsonaro names family, God, Brazil, guns, freedom of expression, and the free market as his banners, then tells ministers who do not accept them that they are in the wrong government. He says ministers praised by critical media should lose their posts. In this formulation, public approval from newspapers or television is not an ordinary measure of performance; it is evidence that a minister may be aligned with the wrong side. The statement makes the president’s relationship with the press part of his internal management of the cabinet.

A recording can preserve force without resolving every dispute about meaning. The April 22 meeting supports Moro’s account that Bolsonaro raised the replacement of security personnel and connected it to his family. It also shows a president who spoke to ministers through a language of enemies, loyalty, and personal grievance. Yet the recording alone does not prove that the Federal Police was redirected to protect a family member, nor does it establish that every minister accepted the president’s framing. Its evidentiary value is narrower and more useful: it shows how the president made a case for his demands in front of the people expected to carry out his government.

That manner of speaking traveled beyond the cabinet. Bolsonaro used social media, live broadcasts, and public appearances to address supporters without relying on the filters of party leaders, established newspapers, or ministerial spokespeople. The direct channel gave him an advantage: he could define an issue in his own terms and present criticism as confirmation that he was challenging a protected elite. For voters who distrusted political parties or conventional journalism, the style could feel like access rather than performance. A president who spoke bluntly, named opponents, and rejected ceremonial language appeared to be speaking as an ordinary citizen who had reached the highest office without surrendering his voice.

The same channel changed the costs of governing. Congress is a coalition legislature, not a single audience waiting to receive a presidential message. Bills require negotiation with party leaders and committee members whose support cannot be secured by addressing voters over their heads. Bolsonaro’s government did pass major legislation, including pension reform, and its eventual relationship with congressional centrão parties became more transactional and pragmatic. That record complicates any claim that confrontation made cooperation impossible. It also shows that when the president’s public posture cast compromise as suspect or treated opponents as enemies, the work of building a durable legislative majority fell to other actors and to bargaining that his rhetoric did not make easier.

Courts faced a similar problem. The Supreme Federal Court and the Superior Electoral Court had constitutional responsibilities that could not be reduced to political opposition, yet Bolsonaro repeatedly framed judicial decisions as interference or hostility. His ministers sometimes echoed that language, as Weintraub did in the April meeting. A president may criticize a court’s reasoning; the danger arises when criticism becomes a standing invitation to doubt the court’s legitimacy whenever it constrains the executive. The press occupied another place in this pattern. Bolsonaro’s attacks could strengthen his bond with supporters who believed mainstream outlets treated him unfairly, while making routine scrutiny appear to them as partisan combat rather than a normal feature of democratic government.

The result was a division between mobilization and administration. Direct communication could keep supporters attentive and give them a shared account of what the president was resisting. It could not, by itself, coordinate the Health Ministry, secure a stable cabinet, or produce trust among officials who feared that disagreement would be recast as disloyalty. The distinction is visible in the contrast between the president’s ability to command public attention and the repeated departures of ministers whose work depended on sustained cooperation. Bolsonaro’s style was not simply a personal manner laid over government. It shaped which relationships were rewarded, which disputes became public, and how much effort had to be spent repairing trust after conflict.

The Independence Day demonstrations of September 7, 2021, brought that tension into the streets. Bolsonaro’s supporters gathered in Brasília and São Paulo, among other cities, for events that joined the national holiday to demands for political change and displays of loyalty to the president. The demonstrations were not a single centrally controlled procession. They were mobilizations by supporters, political allies, and groups that had spent months contesting the authority of the Supreme Federal Court and the reliability of the voting system. Bolsonaro’s speeches gave those grievances a presidential platform.

In Brasília, he spoke to a large crowd and attacked Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who was overseeing investigations involving Bolsonaro’s allies and supporters. Bolsonaro said he would no longer comply with decisions made by the justice. The statement moved beyond criticism of a ruling. It challenged whether the president would obey a court order issued by a member of the Supreme Federal Court. The crowd’s presence amplified the threat: the president was addressing a mass constituency while naming a judge as an adversary, making the dispute appear not as a legal question to be settled through appeal but as a contest between the people and the court.

In São Paulo, Bolsonaro again addressed supporters, with the city’s main avenue serving as a stage for the demonstration. His language there included an attack on the Supreme Federal Court and a warning that the country faced a choice between freedom and tyranny. The speeches did not produce a formal order or a change in the court’s jurisdiction. Their political effect came through the public performance of defiance: a president used the national holiday, a crowd, and the symbols of independence to portray his conflict with a constitutional court as a struggle over national sovereignty.

The response came through political and institutional channels. Leaders in Congress and the Supreme Federal Court condemned the threats, while allies and advisers sought to prevent the confrontation from escalating. Two days later, Bolsonaro issued a written statement in which he said he had not intended to offend or attack the branches of government and described his words as the product of the moment. The retreat mattered because it showed that public pressure and political costs could still induce a change in tone. It did not erase the original speeches, nor did it make the threat to disregard a justice’s decisions less serious.

The demonstrations therefore reveal both the strength and the limits of confrontation as a governing tool. Bolsonaro could gather supporters and use their presence to increase pressure on judges and legislators. But the president’s authority depended on officials continuing to perform their constitutional duties, including judges who could not accept personal threats as a substitute for legal argument. His later conciliation showed that he was not locked into a single rhetorical posture. The episode also showed how quickly a public challenge could damage trust and require a retreat once the costs became clear.

Supporters and critics read this conduct through different political experiences. For many supporters, Bolsonaro’s bluntness was evidence that he had not learned the polished evasions of Brasília. His profanity and insults could signal that he was willing to name what other politicians concealed. The press, the courts, and established parties were not neutral abstractions in this view; they were powerful actors that had often lost public trust. When Bolsonaro attacked them, supporters could see a president refusing to defer to institutions that had not earned their confidence. The April meeting’s complaints about hostile coverage and the September demonstrations’ defense of freedom fit that interpretation.

Critics saw a different pattern in the same episodes. The April meeting did not merely show a president speaking without polish; it showed him tying ministerial service to personal loyalty and describing a route from a security official to the minister when he could not get the change he wanted. Moro’s resignation then placed a specific allegation of interference before the Supreme Federal Court. In September 2021, Bolsonaro did not simply object to a ruling or seek its reversal. He publicly said he would not comply with a justice’s decisions. For critics, this was a question of restraint: whether the president would accept legal limits even when he considered them politically hostile.

The difference is not that one side cared about democracy and the other did not. Supporters often understood themselves to be defending popular sovereignty against institutions they considered insulated from voters. Critics argued that elected authority remained bounded by law and that courts could not be treated as enemies whenever they enforced those bounds. The cases do not make the two positions identical in evidentiary weight. A president’s right to criticize the press or a court is broad; a public threat to disregard judicial decisions has consequences that ordinary criticism does not. Likewise, Moro’s allegations required investigation, but the recording supplied evidence of Bolsonaro’s words rather than proof of every alleged motive.

The strongest defense of Bolsonaro’s style begins with a real democratic point: voters do not lose their voice when they elect a president, and the president need not adopt the manners of a political class many voters distrust. Direct communication can make choices more visible. It can puncture euphemism, expose bureaucratic self-protection, and keep officials responsive to people who feel ignored. The 2018 coalition included voters who wanted security, conservative social policy, economic change, and a break with the Workers’ Party; they did not all share one reason for supporting Bolsonaro. A president who spoke in a recognizable, unscripted voice could maintain a relationship with those voters that conventional political communication often fails to provide.

That case carries weight. Bolsonaro’s government achieved consequential measures, and his ability to mobilize supporters was genuine. Yet candor is not measured only by whether a speaker sounds unfiltered. It also depends on whether the speaker distinguishes evidence from accusation and accepts procedures that constrain his own side. In the April meeting, the president’s concern about family security was joined to a demand for personnel changes that Moro understood as pressure on the Federal Police. In September, the language of popular resistance became a stated refusal to comply with a justice’s decisions. Those acts cannot be reduced to tone. A direct voice may represent voters; it does not exempt the president from the duties attached to the office.

The unresolved question is how much of the gap between mobilization and durable cooperation can be explained by public conduct. Bolsonaro’s words are observable, and the episodes show how they could organize loyalty, intensify conflict, and make retreat costly. They do not reveal every private negotiation or every administrative failure. Nor can they tell us how the same coalition might have governed under a less confrontational president. The record leaves a narrower question: when a leader’s strongest political asset is the ability to make supporters feel represented against powerful opponents, how can that asset be used without making cooperation with those opponents—and with the officials required to govern—seem like betrayal?
