chapters.markdown:
On January 8, 2023, demonstrators invaded and ransacked the seats of Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies, Federal Senate, presidential palace and Supreme Federal Court in Brasília. Five former members of the senior leadership of the Federal District Military Police were later held responsible for failing in their duties by allowing demonstrators access to Praça dos Três Poderes and the vandalism of the buildings.

Later, Justice Alexandre de Moraes reported that 1,399 people had been held criminally responsible for the attacks. Those convicted included former president Jair Bolsonaro and 28 former members of his government, found guilty of planning an attempted coup to prevent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva from taking office.

Some defendants received non-prosecution agreements. They had been charged only with incitement and criminal association, and had camped outside military barracks; there was no evidence that they had taken part in the attempted coup, obstructed the branches of government or damaged public property.

Brazil’s electronic voting system was designed to make the count faster and reduce familiar vulnerabilities in paper ballots: delayed tallies, invalid votes, and opportunities for interference during transport and counting. Electronic voting began in 1996 and was used nationwide by 2000. The Superior Electoral Court, or TSE, supervises the process from voter registration through certification. Its role is unusually direct: the same national court sets procedures, organizes the election, and announces the results. That concentration invites scrutiny, but it also makes the chain of responsibility identifiable.

The machines do not connect to the internet while votes are cast. Before an election, their software is tested and inspected under procedures open to political parties and other authorized observers. At the close of voting, each machine produces a printed record of its local tally, while the electronic results are transmitted for aggregation. These safeguards do not make a system infallible. They do mean that a claim of fraud needs to identify a plausible route by which votes were altered, and evidence that the route was used.

Bolsonaro’s objections were not all of the same kind. Concerns about transparency, auditability, and public confidence are legitimate subjects for debate; a voting system should be capable of explaining how it works and how its results can be checked. His proposals for printed ballots or printed records also entered a political contest over how much independent verification voters should have. Congress rejected a constitutional amendment requiring printed ballots, and the Supreme Federal Court ruled an earlier law unconstitutional, citing cost and risks to ballot secrecy. Those decisions did not prove that every feature of the existing system was beyond improvement. They did reject a particular remedy.

The more consequential claim was that electronic voting had been manipulated. Bolsonaro repeatedly alleged fraud without producing evidence that votes had been changed. In July 2022, he brought foreign diplomats to the Palácio da Alvorada and presented allegations about the electoral system, including a hacker intrusion into the electoral authority’s internal network in 2018. The TSE’s account of that intrusion was specific: the hacker had not accessed the voting machines or their source code and could not alter the vote totals. A breach of an internal system deserved investigation; it did not establish that ballots had been changed.

The distinction between a security concern and proof of a stolen election is not technical pedantry. It is the difference between asking officials to demonstrate safeguards and telling voters that their choices may not count. The TSE’s procedures could be questioned, and its decisions could be challenged through legal channels. But the public allegations moved beyond the identified vulnerability to a conclusion for which no supporting evidence was produced. Bolsonaro had also won the presidency through the same electronic system in 2018. That earlier result did not certify every later procedure, but it made his selective distrust harder to separate from political advantage.

The result in 2022 would be close enough to make scrutiny especially important. It would also be clear enough, once the count was complete, to give the losing campaign a precise fact to confront.

On October 30, the TSE’s second-round count gave Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva 50.90 percent of valid votes and Jair Bolsonaro 49.10 percent. Lula received 60,345,999 votes; Bolsonaro received 58,206,354. The difference was 2,139,645 votes. A narrow margin is not an invitation to treat uncertainty as evidence. It is a reason to look closely at the count, the procedures, and the claims made about them.

The official tally recorded 123,682,372 valid votes. Blank ballots numbered 1,964,779 and null ballots 3,487,874; 32,770,982 voters abstained. Those figures describe different choices and circumstances. Abstention is not a vote against either candidate, and blank or null ballots do not belong in the denominator of valid votes. The percentages that decided the presidency were calculated from the valid ballots cast.

Lula’s victory completed a contest between a former president returning to office and an incumbent seeking another term. His lead was smaller than Bolsonaro’s 2018 margin, but the count did not leave the presidency undecided. The TSE certified the result after the electoral process, and the certification made Lula president-elect. That institutional act mattered because it converted a count into a lawful outcome, binding on both campaigns whether or not either welcomed it.

The result also preserved the difference between electoral victory and political mandate. Lula had won the office, but nearly half of the valid electorate had voted for Bolsonaro. The size of that opposition could not undo the count; nor could the count make the opposition disappear. Any account of the transition has to hold both facts together: a decisive constitutional result and a country divided almost evenly between the candidates.

Bolsonaro did not explicitly acknowledge the result. He authorized the transition, while his public silence left supporters and officials to read meaning into what he had not said. The silence did not erase the certification. It did, however, leave a question that the formal result could not settle: how far could a party go in contesting the count before a demand for verification became an effort to discredit the election itself?

The Liberal Party’s petition of November 22 gave that question a concrete form. The party, led by Valdemar Costa Neto and supporting Bolsonaro’s candidacy, asked the TSE to invalidate votes from about 280,000 electronic machines used in the runoff. Its filing alleged that five older models had displayed technical irregularities and relied on a report by Instituto Voto Legal, hired by the party. The requested remedy was not a recount of a small set of disputed precincts. It was invalidation of the votes cast on the machines in question, a step that would have changed the outcome.

The party’s lawyer, Marcelo Bessa, described the alleged inconsistencies as a possible vulnerability, not proof that fraud had occurred. That qualification is important. A technical anomaly may warrant investigation, but a possibility of weakness does not demonstrate that the weakness was exploited, much less that it changed the winner. The petition’s own proposed calculation assumed that votes from the machines should be discarded and then projected a different result. The assumption did the work that evidence needed to do.

Alexandre de Moraes, then president of the TSE, pointed out that the machines identified in the petition had been used in both rounds. If the party’s concern applied to those models, it could not coherently target only the second round. He ordered the Liberal Party to amend its filing within twenty-four hours to include the first round as well, warning that otherwise the petition would be rejected. The party did not comply. Moraes rejected the request and imposed a fine, finding that the filing had been made in bad faith and ordered the party to pay 22.9 million reais.

The court’s ruling did not establish that every machine was incapable of malfunction. It established that the petition had not provided a basis for the extraordinary remedy it sought, and that its selective treatment of the second round was untenable once the same models’ use in the first round was acknowledged. The party’s allegations remained allegations; the court accepted no evidence that the machines had altered votes.

A legal challenge can be part of democratic contestation. It can also be used to give an unsupported claim the appearance of a substantiated case. The November petition was filed by Bolsonaro’s party, not by Bolsonaro personally, though it sought to overturn the result that had removed him from office. The distinction in authorship matters. So does the distinction between a party’s assertion and a court’s finding.

After the petition failed, the transition proceeded under the pressure of a result that Bolsonaro had not explicitly conceded. His authorization for the handover allowed government work to begin, but his silence and his earlier attacks on the voting system left room for supporters to interpret the election as unresolved. Across the country, demonstrators blocked roads and camped outside military facilities. Some demanded military intervention. Their presence reflected real anger and distrust among Bolsonaro voters, but the demand for intervention crossed a line that ordinary protest does not.

The transition had practical work to do. Lula’s team needed access to federal information and the cooperation of ministries; Bolsonaro’s administration had to prepare for a change of government. The handover took place, and Lula assumed office on January 1, 2023. Bolsonaro left Brazil before the inauguration and was in Florida. His departure avoided the customary transfer ceremony, a public gesture that would have recognized the successor even if he remained a political opponent.

The road blockades affected people who had not chosen to join the protests. They interrupted travel and commerce, while encampments outside barracks kept alive the hope that the armed forces might stop the transfer. These acts were not identical. A peaceful gathering to express distrust of the count remained protected political speech; blocking roads imposed costs on others, and calling for military intervention challenged the constitutional process. The state’s response had to distinguish among them rather than treat every dissenter as a conspirator.

That distinction became harder to maintain after the attacks in Brasília. The consequences reached beyond the damaged buildings and the immediate criminal cases. The invasion exposed failures in the Federal District’s security arrangements, and the Supreme Federal Court and Congress faced the task of separating responsibility for those failures from responsibility for planning or carrying out an attempt to prevent the new government from exercising power.

The Federal District Military Police came under investigation, and senior officers faced scrutiny over the security operation. The inquiry examined what officials had known, what they had done, and whether omissions had allowed the breach. Five former members of the force’s senior leadership were later held responsible for failing in their duties. Their cases concerned the conduct of public officers, not the political beliefs of everyone who had protested outside military barracks.

The distinction shaped the broader proceedings. Prosecutors and investigators considered different levels of participation: people accused of entering and damaging public buildings; people charged with supporting or organizing the effort; and officials or political figures alleged to have helped prepare a break with constitutional government. The evidence required for each category differed. Presence at a protest did not itself prove participation in a conspiracy, while public support for intervention could be relevant without proving that the speaker planned an attack.

The political consequences were also immediate. Lula’s government and Congress had to respond to an assault on the transfer of power while avoiding the appearance that criticism of the new administration would itself be treated as criminal. The Supreme Federal Court, whose own building had been attacked, became central to investigations and trials. That role drew criticism about the concentration of judicial power, but the court’s involvement did not make every allegation against a defendant true. Each case still required evidence and a ruling.

Over time, the legal response produced sharply different outcomes. Many defendants received penalties of up to a year or entered non-prosecution agreements. Those agreements were available to people charged only with incitement and criminal association, whose presence at encampments did not prove that they had taken part in the attempted coup, obstructed the branches of government, or damaged public property. More serious cases led to longer prison terms. The categories mattered because they prevented the broadest accusation from swallowing the differences among individual conduct.

The figures later reported by Alexandre de Moraes—1,399 people held criminally responsible—covered a range of cases and outcomes, not a single finding about a single group. Some judgments were final; others remained subject to appeals or further proceedings. Allegations against Bolsonaro and former officials had to be distinguished from convictions, and convictions from judgments that had completed every stage of review. A court’s sentence carries legal force, but the status of each case depends on its procedural history.

For Bolsonaro, the post-election period did not end with the transfer of office. The TSE’s separate decision in June 2023 found him ineligible to stand for office for eight years because of his use of government channels to attack the electoral system before the election. That was an electoral judgment about abuse of political power and misuse of media, not a criminal conviction for the events in Brasília. Keeping those proceedings separate is necessary to understand both their legal basis and their consequences.

Supporters of the post-election protests had a serious argument available to them. In a democracy, voters may distrust officials, question election procedures, demand audits, and assemble in public. Brazil’s political history gives many citizens reasons to fear that powerful actors can evade accountability. The TSE’s control over electoral administration, however carefully designed, should not be exempt from scrutiny. A close result can intensify doubts, and peaceful protest is not evidence of disloyalty.

That case deserves to be heard. It does not make every claim made in its name credible. The Liberal Party’s petition did not show that votes had been changed; it sought to discard results from machines used in both rounds while initially challenging only the second. The court’s demand to include the first round exposed the weakness in that approach. The party’s allegations about older machines did not become proof simply because they were put in a legal filing.

Nor does the right to protest cover every method of protest. A march, a vigil, or a public demand for an audit belongs to ordinary democratic life. A blockade can interfere with the rights of people who are not participating, and a demand that the armed forces prevent an elected president from taking office is not simply a request for better verification. Once violence and damage entered the process, the question was no longer only whether demonstrators had a right to be angry. It was also whether particular people had committed crimes and whether officials had failed in duties they were legally bound to perform.

The answer cannot be that everyone who supported Bolsonaro shared responsibility for the attacks. Millions voted for him, and many rejected the result without participating in unlawful conduct. Nor can the answer be that a political leader bears no responsibility unless a court finds him guilty of a specific offense. Presidents shape the terms in which supporters understand public events. Bolsonaro’s repeated, unsupported claims about electronic voting helped establish a climate in which an adverse result could be treated as suspect before the count was complete. That political contribution is not identical to criminal liability, but it belongs in an assessment of his presidency.

The evidentiary boundaries are plain even when the politics are not. The TSE’s certified count established Lula’s victory. The Liberal Party’s petition documented an effort to challenge that result, not proof that fraud had changed it. The road protests included lawful dissent and conduct that interfered with public life; the calls for military intervention rejected the constitutional transfer. The later cases assigned responsibility according to evidence and individual conduct, with different charges, agreements, and sentences.

Bolsonaro’s supporters were not wrong to expect a president to defend their interests, or to scrutinize the machinery of an election. They were entitled to demand explanations. Bolsonaro, as president, was also responsible for the effects of his own public conduct. His refusal to make a clear, timely acknowledgment of the certified result, following years of attacks on the voting system, left distrust politically useful and institutionally costly. The transfer of power went ahead, but it did not pass without damage to confidence in the rules that made the transfer legitimate.

chapters.markdown:
In 2018, Bolsonaro’s registered program offered broad signals: security, economic change, national sovereignty, and social conservatism. Four years later, his reelection plan, filed with the Superior Electoral Court, did something different. It made the presidency itself its principal evidence. Titled *For the Good of Brazil*, the document presented programs already under way as reasons to continue the government and placed the defense of its record beside the promise of a conservative agenda. The word “family” appeared sixty-seven times. Freedom occupied the opening chapter, defined through family, democracy, economic liberty, property, the right to life of the unborn, and the right to express opinions and live by one’s values.

That shift from promise to defense is useful for judging the administration on its own terms. A program written for reelection is not an audit, and its emphasis cannot show how well a policy worked. But it does reveal what Bolsonaro’s campaign chose to make central at the end of his term. The 2022 plan did not chiefly ask voters to imagine a new government. It asked them to preserve the one they had.

The official 2018 program had made room for a wide coalition. Its ambitions included economic liberalization and public security, alongside national and social themes that could speak to voters with different priorities. The later document narrowed the focus to continuity and identity. Its repeated language of freedom connected economic choice to religious and moral convictions, while its account of government emphasized programs already operating. The campaign’s argument was that these aims belonged together: a government that defended family and individual liberty could also claim credit for economic reform and public administration.

Some of that record was concrete. Congress enacted Constitutional Amendment No. 103 in 2019, changing federal retirement rules after negotiations that depended on congressional leaders as well as the administration. The Economic Freedom Law reduced licensing requirements for low-risk activities. The federal government expanded digital access to services through gov.br, and Eletrobras was privatized in 2022 through a share offering, with the state retaining a special voting right. These were consequential changes, though they did not amount to the wholesale retreat of the state that some supporters had hoped for. Banco do Brasil remained public, and the broader program of privatization and investment did not advance at the scale implied by the campaign’s economic ambitions.

The same test applies to the plan’s language of freedom. A government may defend religious conviction and property rights while also being judged by whether it protects the conditions under which citizens can exercise rights equally. In the Amazon, rising deforestation and weaker enforcement damaged the government’s claim to have balanced development with stewardship. Indigenous land protections became a site of conflict rather than a settled guarantee. The administration did not abolish environmental agencies, but its public signals and policy choices made enforcement less credible. The difference between a stated priority and a governing result was visible in the distance between the language of sovereignty and the practical loss of confidence among Brazil’s partners.

The pandemic exposed a sharper gap. Bolsonaro’s government created emergency assistance, initially set at R$600 a month for eligible recipients after Congress raised the administration’s proposed amount, and supported the AstraZeneca-Fiocruz vaccine partnership. Those actions mattered to millions of people. Yet the federal response also included repeated presidential opposition to broad restrictions, conflict with governors, and consequential delays in vaccine procurement. Shared public-health responsibilities did not remove the federal government’s power to coordinate purchases or communicate risk. The 2022 program’s emphasis on continuity asked voters to treat these choices as part of a successful record, but the record was mixed by the administration’s own conduct.

The reelection plan deserves attention without being mistaken for a verdict. It tells us how Bolsonaro wanted the final years of his government understood: as the defense of freedom, family, and conservative change, joined to a claim of practical continuity. Whether the government delivered those aims, or whether its achievements outweighed the costs of its conflicts, must be judged through enacted measures and their consequences, not the campaign’s preferred description.

The presidency’s political meaning was tested after Bolsonaro left office, when a dispute over his public conduct became a case before Brazil’s electoral court. On June 30, 2023, the Superior Electoral Court, sitting in Brasília, found him ineligible to stand for office for eight years. The case concerned his meeting with foreign ambassadors at the presidential residence on July 18, 2022, and his attacks on the reliability of Brazil’s electronic voting system.

The meeting was not a private conversation. Bolsonaro used his position as president to address ambassadors accredited to Brazil and discuss the country’s election system before the October vote. He repeated claims that electronic voting was vulnerable and cast doubt on the system’s reliability, though he did not present evidence to substantiate the allegations. Public television broadcast the event, and it circulated widely. Its setting mattered: foreign representatives were being asked to hear a president challenge the machinery through which his own mandate would be renewed.

The TSE’s case proceeded under electoral law, not as a general judgment on Bolsonaro’s politics. The court considered whether the meeting and the use of presidential communication had abused political power and the means of communication, giving Bolsonaro an unfair advantage and damaging the equality of the contest. It did not need to prove that any vote had been altered. The question was the conduct of a candidate who was also the sitting president, the reach of the event, and its capacity to distort the conditions of the election.

Benedito Gonçalves, the rapporteur, presented the case to the court. The majority concluded that Bolsonaro had used the authority and visibility of his office to spread unsupported attacks on the voting system in a setting that magnified their effect. The court found him responsible for abuse of political power and misuse of the media, and imposed ineligibility for eight years, counted from the 2022 election. The ruling did not remove him from office retroactively, overturn the election result, or declare that his supporters had committed wrongdoing merely by believing his claims.

Electoral law protects more than the accuracy of a count after voting has ended; it also protects the fairness of the contest while voters are deciding. A president has access to official platforms and public attention unavailable to an ordinary candidate. When he uses those advantages to undermine confidence in the electoral process without substantiation, the issue is not simply whether voters were persuaded. It is whether the contest was conducted on equal terms and whether public power was used for a candidate’s benefit.

The ruling was not the last word in every legal matter involving Bolsonaro, and its sanction did not settle the broader political dispute. The June 2023 decision nevertheless established a specific legal finding about a specific event: Bolsonaro’s meeting with ambassadors and his attacks on the voting system violated electoral rules in a way that justified a period of ineligibility. That finding concerns the conduct and sanction in this case; it does not amount to a complete account of his presidency.

Bolsonaro and his supporters treated the decision as political persecution, arguing that the court had punished a leader for raising questions about election security. Their argument draws force from a real democratic principle: public officials and candidates may scrutinize electoral procedures, and courts should not convert criticism into an offense merely because it is unwelcome. Brazil’s voting system is not beyond question simply because it is electronic, and public confidence cannot be commanded by decree.

But the TSE’s finding was not that any criticism of electronic voting was unlawful. The case concerned the president’s use of a formal meeting with foreign ambassadors to repeat claims without evidence, in the months before an election in which he was a candidate. The legal question was whether that conduct abused his office and the communication advantages attached to it. The political claim of persecution addresses the legitimacy of the court and the meaning of the sanction; it does not erase the conduct the court examined.

Nor does the legal ruling prove every broader criticism made of Bolsonaro. It does not establish that every supporter was hostile to democracy, or that every political appeal to distrust was criminal. It identifies a narrower responsibility: a sitting president used a high-profile official event to attack the voting system and was found to have violated electoral law. A political leader may call the decision unjust; that response remains part of political debate.

The two kinds of judgment answer different questions. The TSE determined whether the conduct met the legal standard for abuse and what sanction followed. Supporters’ arguments ask whether the court’s decision was fair, whether scrutiny of elections is being chilled, and whether the sanction will exclude a popular figure from political competition. Those questions deserve consideration, but they cannot substitute for the court’s findings about the event. Conversely, the legal judgment cannot by itself settle the quality of Bolsonaro’s whole presidency.

His political reach remained measurable, though not in a way that can be reduced to a single vote total. In October 2024, Brazilians elected mayors and municipal councillors across the country. The results showed that conservative and right-wing parties remained powerful, while individual candidates’ performance varied from city to city. Bolsonaro endorsed candidates in several contests; some won and others lost. A vote for an endorsed mayoral candidate, however, is not a direct ballot for Bolsonaro. Local contests turn on municipal services, alliances, party organization, and the standing of the candidate as well as national politics.

The first round gave the Liberal Party, Bolsonaro’s party, a strong position in many municipalities and made it one of the leading forces in the mayoral contests. In São Paulo, Bolsonaro backed Ricardo Nunes, the incumbent, who advanced to the runoff and won. The result showed the value of Bolsonaro’s endorsement when attached to a candidate with an existing municipal coalition and a broad base of support. It did not show that every voter for Nunes was voting to restore Bolsonaro to the presidency. Nunes had his own record, allies, and reasons for attracting votes.

Other contests made the limits clearer. In some cities, Bolsonaro’s preferred candidate failed to advance or lost, despite the national attention attached to the endorsement. Municipal elections reward organization that can reach voters repeatedly and assemble local alliances; a national figure can help mobilize supporters, but may also make a race more polarizing. The outcome depends on the candidate and the city.

The results also cannot be read as a direct measure of the 2022 presidential electorate. Voters choose a mayor to manage local services and a president to lead the country; turnout and candidate selection differ. Party success can reflect a coalition’s strength without proving personal loyalty to its most prominent figure. Bolsonaro remained an influential endorser, but the 2024 results did not confer on him an independent mandate, nor did they test him as a candidate.

They did show that his political network had not disappeared after the election loss and the TSE ruling. The Liberal Party, allied conservative parties, and local candidates could still draw on the constituency that had supported him. His influence was real but mediated: it operated through endorsements, party ties, and the continued appeal of a political identity, rather than through a direct national vote in 2024. That distinction matters when assessing both the durability of his movement and the limits imposed by his legal status.

The strongest case made by Bolsonaro’s supporters begins with representation. For years, many voters felt that the political class treated their moral views, concerns about crime, and distrust of the Workers’ Party as backward or illegitimate. Bolsonaro spoke in a language that did not ask them to soften those convictions before entering public life. He made conservative Christians, security-minded voters, and people hostile to the established left feel that their preferences could shape national policy. This was not an illusion created by one man alone; it reflected a durable coalition and a genuine demand for political recognition.

Supporters can also point to changes that were more than symbolic. Pension reform altered the federal system, the Economic Freedom Law reduced some barriers for low-risk businesses, and digital services expanded. Eletrobras’s privatization changed the ownership structure of a major state-controlled company. The administration’s emergency assistance reached eligible households during the economic shock of the pandemic, while the AstraZeneca-Fiocruz partnership contributed to vaccine supply. These measures were not all designed or passed by Bolsonaro personally, but they occurred under his government and form part of its record.

A serious judgment should grant that record. Bolsonaro was not an empty vessel, and his voters were not simply deceived. The reform agenda produced lasting legal changes; his government also made choices that supporters understood as defending national sovereignty and resisting a political establishment they distrusted. The president’s direct style could appear to them as candour, especially compared with leaders who spoke in polished abstractions while seeming remote from ordinary concerns.

Yet representation cannot be the only measure of a presidency. A president who gives neglected voters a voice remains responsible for how he uses the office and what his administration accomplishes. The pension reform required sustained congressional work, and its passage depended on legislators who were not merely extensions of the president. By contrast, the broader promises of privatization and investment were unevenly delivered. The government’s environmental record weakened enforcement while deforestation rose. During COVID-19, emergency aid and vaccine support coexisted with public resistance to restrictions and delays in procurement. These are not minor qualifications to a record of success; they are part of its substance.

Nor does the argument from representation excuse attacks on the electoral system. A leader may question procedures and demand answers, but a president’s unsupported claims carry a weight that ordinary criticism does not. The TSE ruling addressed a particular use of presidential power, not the beliefs of millions of voters. This distinction allows supporters’ grievances to be heard without treating every legal finding as partisan punishment, and it allows criticism of Bolsonaro without denying that his constituency had legitimate political demands.

The supporter case is strongest when it insists that voters chose a real program and that the administration enacted consequential reforms. It is weakest when it treats popular identification as proof of administrative success or institutional innocence. The same presidency could represent people who had felt excluded, pass important economic measures, and still fail to coordinate effectively in a national emergency or protect confidence in democratic procedures. Recognition is a political achievement; it is not a substitute for governing.

Political appeal and administrative effectiveness are related, but they are not interchangeable. Bolsonaro’s appeal rested partly on his ability to speak directly to voters who believed conventional politics had ignored them. His plain, combative language made conflict itself seem like evidence of authenticity. He could present a dispute with judges, journalists, governors, or international critics as a contest between ordinary citizens and powerful interests. That style strengthened identification. It did not necessarily help the government carry policy through.

The pension reform illustrates the difference. Its passage required negotiation with Congress, especially with Rodrigo Maia and other legislators who could assemble votes. The reform was consequential, but its success depended on bargaining and legislative work that did not arise from presidential confrontation alone. Bolsonaro could claim the result as part of his administration’s record; he could not plausibly treat it as proof that personal conflict was an effective substitute for coalition-building.

The pandemic showed the costs more starkly. Brazil’s public-health system distributed responsibilities among the Union, states, and municipalities, and the Supreme Federal Court affirmed that local governments could act within their powers. That division did not leave the federal government powerless. The Ministry of Health negotiated national purchases, and the federal government could coordinate information and procurement. Bolsonaro’s public opposition to broad restrictions, his conflicts with governors, and delays in accepting early Pfizer offers weakened the coherence of the national response. Emergency aid and vaccine partnerships were real achievements, but they do not erase the consequences of those choices.

Administrative effectiveness also requires attention to continuity. Frequent changes among senior officials and public disputes over policy made it harder to maintain a stable direction, even where capable officials and agencies continued their work. The environmental record showed how a government could retain formal agencies while diminishing the credibility of enforcement. The question is not whether Bolsonaro had a popular mandate or whether some policies succeeded, but whether his administration could convert political support into sustained, coordinated results.

On that measure, the record is uneven. The government delivered a major pension reform, changed rules for low-risk businesses, expanded digital services, and supported emergency assistance. It also fell short of important economic promises, weakened environmental accountability, and responded to COVID-19 with a mixture of useful programs and damaging conflict. The contrast is not between a popular leader and an unpopular bureaucracy. It is between the capacity to mobilize support and the capacity to make the state act coherently over time.

Bolsonaro’s public conduct repeatedly favoured immediacy: direct messages, public challenges, and sharp divisions between allies and opponents. That approach could keep supporters engaged and force neglected issues into debate. It also made cooperation more difficult when success depended on trust among the presidency, Congress, courts, state governments, and technical agencies. The result was not failure everywhere. His achievements were clearest where institutions and legislators could carry work forward; his weaknesses grew more consequential when coordination and credible communication were essential.

The unresolved question is how far those observable habits explain the unevenness. Bolsonaro could accept congressional bargaining when a major reform required it, yet often treated other disagreements as public contests in which compromise risked appearing as surrender. That pattern is visible in the record; a private motive is not needed to describe it. Does it reflect a durable limit on his ability to build coalitions, or a political method that succeeds when supporters reward confrontation and fails when government requires continuity across institutions?

The question reaches beyond one administration because the coalition Bolsonaro assembled did not vanish with his defeat. Conservative parties retained local strength, candidates continued to seek his endorsement, and his public voice remained influential even after the TSE judgment. At the same time, the 2024 municipal results showed that influence had to pass through local candidates and alliances. A national leader could help define a contest without controlling its outcome.

His political future also depends on legal proceedings and the choices of other politicians. The eight-year ineligibility ruling sharply constrained his ability to run for office under its terms, while leaving open the possibility that his supporters could organize around other candidates. Whether those candidates can hold together a coalition spanning religious conservatives, security voters, business interests, and anti-left voters is not settled by Bolsonaro’s continuing popularity, or by the fact that some of his preferred candidates won municipal office.

A portrait of his influence must therefore include both presence and dependence. Bolsonaro remains a recognizable national figure whose endorsements can matter, but his political reach is mediated by party leaders, local candidates, and voters who may share some of his priorities without accepting every position he takes. The 2024 contests demonstrated that his movement could compete without converting every race into a personal referendum. They also showed that local organization and candidate credibility could matter more than a presidential endorsement.

The presidency leaves a harder measure. Bolsonaro’s rise gave political force to voters who felt disrespected by established parties, and his administration enacted reforms that will outlast the term. His direct style made that representation vivid. It also made cooperation less reliable and weakened trust at moments when national coordination mattered most. The COVID-19 response and the attacks on the voting system cannot be reduced to personality, but his public conduct was part of their political conditions and consequences.

His influence may endure as a movement, a set of policy commitments, and a language of opposition. Whether it endures as a governing project depends on what its leaders do when they must bargain, administer, and accept constraints. The judgment of Bolsonaro’s presidency is therefore not that popularity was false or achievement absent. Representation and reform were real; the costs of confrontation became clearest when Brazil needed a president to coordinate the country and sustain confidence in its rules.

Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the abdomen on the afternoon of September 6, 2018, during a campaign event in Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais. He was rushed to a local hospital and underwent emergency surgery. The operation controlled internal bleeding from five wounds: one in the mesenteric artery, one in the large intestine and three in the small intestine. Doctors performed a colostomy. Bolsonaro, 63, was stable in intensive care but remained at risk and could not yet be transferred; his recovery was expected to take three to four weeks.

Adélio Bispo de Oliveira, 40, was identified as the attacker and arrested at the scene. He told police he had stabbed Bolsonaro for personal reasons and in the name of God.

Authorities and other presidential hopefuls reacted immediately, including Bolsonaro’s fiercest rivals.

The registered plan titled *O Caminho da Prosperidade* offered a formal outline of what Jair Bolsonaro said he would do in government. It was a compact document, less a detailed program for administration than a set of commitments arranged under broad headings: security, economic freedom, social questions, and a state presented as burdened by corruption and inefficiency. Its title, “The Path to Prosperity,” made a national promise. The text’s political work was to give that promise a recognizable direction without requiring every supporter to agree on the route.

On security, the plan joined public order to the rights of citizens and the freedom to defend themselves. Bolsonaro’s campaign statements sharpened that language. He advocated loosening restrictions on gun ownership and giving police greater latitude in confronting suspected criminals. He also spoke of deploying the military against crime. The proposals addressed a country where homicide and robbery were not abstractions, and where many voters saw the state as failing to protect them. But they did not amount to a single operational blueprint. The platform named a posture; the campaign’s sharper declarations supplied its force.

The economic pages made a different appeal. They promised privatization, lower barriers to enterprise, and a reduction in the reach of the state. Paulo Guedes, the economist who became the campaign’s principal economic adviser, gave these commitments a market-oriented vocabulary. To business audiences and voters who blamed public spending and political patronage for stagnation, the language suggested a break with the economic policies associated with the Workers’ Party. Yet the plan did not settle every question about how quickly privatization would proceed, which state companies would be sold, or how the costs of adjustment would be distributed. Its clarity lay in direction, not in a complete map.

The social language was more categorical. Bolsonaro opposed abortion and same-sex marriage and invoked the traditional family as a national value. That position could be heard as a promise to defend religious conviction against a cultural elite believed to be indifferent or hostile to it. It also reached beyond church membership: voters who did not identify as evangelical could share opposition to the Workers’ Party, support for conservative social norms, or distrust of rapid cultural change. The plan’s vocabulary bundled those concerns together, while the people who responded to it did not necessarily hold them in equal measure.

Its anti-corruption promise carried an especially strong political charge. The campaign presented Bolsonaro as clean in contrast with a political class discredited by the Lava Jato investigations and the scandals surrounding established parties. He supported the proposed Ten Measures Against Corruption and spoke as though personal distance from the old political order could itself guarantee a different kind of government. The claim was persuasive as a contrast, but a presidential program required more than the candidate’s self-presentation: it required rules, appointments, legislative partners, and a willingness to accept constraints. The plan named the desired virtue more plainly than it described the work of making it durable.

That gap did not make the platform meaningless. A government plan filed with the TSE was a public commitment, and its language mattered. It told voters which concerns Bolsonaro’s campaign would elevate and which kinds of change it would call legitimate. But it cannot be read as a transcript of the coalition’s collective wishes. An evangelical voter might have placed family policy first; a police officer, public security; an investor, privatization; an anti-PT voter, the defeat of a party associated with corruption. Many could support the same candidate for different reasons, and some could disagree with parts of the plan while treating the election as a choice between political camps.

The document’s broadness was therefore both a limitation and a political asset. It left unresolved questions that would become consequential in office, but it allowed a coalition to assemble around direction, identity, and opposition before its members had to agree on administrative detail. Bolsonaro’s campaign offered a common adversary and a set of signals. It did not offer one common account of what prosperity, order, or family protection would require in every policy area.

The signals were repeated in different registers, each aimed at a constituency that could recognize its own grievance without being asked to share every other voter’s priorities. Public security came first in the campaign’s emotional vocabulary. Bolsonaro promised easier access to guns, stronger police powers, and a more forceful response to crime. Men were particularly receptive to his security appeal, but fear of violence was not confined to male voters, nor did support for tougher policing imply agreement on every proposal. For many, the promise began with a simple judgment: the state had not kept people safe.

Corruption supplied a second signal. Bolsonaro attacked the established parties and associated the Workers’ Party with the scandals exposed during Lava Jato. He presented himself as an incorruptible outsider, though he had spent decades in Congress. The appeal depended less on absence from politics than on a claim to stand outside the political class that voters blamed. Anti-PT voters could hear in it a promise to punish a party they opposed; others heard a general demand for cleaner government.

Social conservatism addressed evangelical Christians and a wider public uneasy with changes in family and gender politics. Opposition to abortion and same-sex marriage, alongside the language of faith and traditional family, made the campaign legible to religious voters who wanted their moral commitments represented in national politics. Evangelical communities were not a single bloc, however. Pastors, congregations, and individual voters differed in their political judgments, and religious identity did not dictate a vote.

National identity gave these messages a shared frame. Bolsonaro’s military background and praise for order offered some voters a language of patriotism, discipline, and national restoration. The same symbols unsettled others, especially those who associated military rule with repression. His running mate, General Hamilton Mourão, reinforced the campaign’s military associations, while Bolsonaro’s opponents argued that his rhetoric threatened democratic norms.

The economic message completed the inventory without resolving its tensions. Privatization and a smaller state appealed to business interests and voters who favored market reform; the promise of security and state force appealed to voters who wanted government to act more aggressively. Those positions could coexist in a campaign because they answered different frustrations. Their compatibility in governing would be harder to assume.

The campaign did not need every supporter to share one theory of Brazil’s problems. It needed each group to recognize a reason to vote for the same candidate, and a reason to believe that the alternative was worse.

The communication system helped make that coalition visible to itself. Bolsonaro used social media and messaging applications, especially WhatsApp, to circulate statements directly to supporters and to encourage their further distribution. The candidate could appear without the filtering conventions of a press conference or a newspaper interview. A short video, a forwarded message, or a post could carry a political identity as much as a policy proposal: the speaker was not merely making a claim but refusing the manners and gatekeeping associated with established media.

That directness strengthened the anti-establishment appeal, but it did not mean conventional news coverage had become irrelevant. Newspapers and television continued to report the campaign, scrutinize its statements, and provide a common arena in which candidates could be compared. Bolsonaro’s attacks on the press could themselves become news, giving his conflict with journalists a second life beyond the original exchange. Coverage that criticized him might reach voters who saw it as evidence of bias; coverage that repeated his claims might extend their reach. The old and new channels were not separate systems. They fed one another.

The campaign’s advantage was not simply that social media bypassed editors. It was that the candidate’s public style fit a medium in which sharp conflict traveled easily. A direct accusation against the political class could be clipped and shared; a conventional interview could be recast as proof that the press was hostile. Supporters did not need to accept every claim to value the posture. The communication offered recognition: the candidate spoke as though he were addressing people whom established politicians had ignored and established journalists misunderstood.

This pattern had limits. WhatsApp groups were not a reliable census of the electorate, and the circulation of a message did not prove that every recipient believed it. The campaign’s reach also depended on older political networks, religious communities, family ties, and the news attention that helped make Bolsonaro a national figure. Digital communication could accelerate and personalize the campaign, but it could not by itself explain why the messages resonated. The recession, corruption scandals, insecurity, and hostility to the Workers’ Party gave them an audience.

Nor did direct communication necessarily produce a shared program. A voter receiving a message about guns might support Bolsonaro for security while knowing little about privatization; a business supporter might welcome Guedes while disliking the candidate’s social rhetoric. The same channel could bind people to a leader while leaving their policy priorities distinct. That combination—personal identification without full agreement—was central to the coalition’s strength and would later complicate claims that the result endorsed every promise equally.

After the attack in Juiz de Fora, the campaign changed its form. Bolsonaro could no longer conduct the ordinary sequence of public rallies and face-to-face appearances on which a candidate might rely. His recovery and hospitalization narrowed his physical campaign, while his supporters and advisers continued to circulate his message. The interruption did not erase the campaign’s existing networks; it made the candidate’s absence from public events part of the immediate political landscape.

The first round on October 7 placed Bolsonaro ahead of Fernando Haddad, the Workers’ Party candidate, with 46.03 percent of valid votes to Haddad’s 29.28 percent. The result established that Bolsonaro had entered the runoff with a substantial lead, not that the election was settled. The second round required him to attract voters whose first choices had been eliminated, including people who had supported other conservative candidates and those whose principal aim was to prevent a Workers’ Party return.

His reduced public schedule also changed the balance between the candidate’s own appearances and mediated communication. Supporters could share messages and images without waiting for a rally; television coverage continued to frame the contest for viewers who were not members of campaign networks. The campaign’s direct style had already made Bolsonaro a familiar figure. The period after Juiz de Fora tested whether that familiarity could sustain a national candidacy when the candidate could not campaign in the usual way.

The immediate political consequence was not a single conversion of sympathy into votes. The attack intensified attention, but Bolsonaro’s support had been built before it, through security, anti-corruption, social conservatism, and rejection of the Workers’ Party. Treating the event as the cause of his victory would erase those earlier alignments; treating it as irrelevant would ignore how abruptly it altered the campaign’s public rhythm. The runoff was won through a coalition that existed before the interruption and continued to operate through channels that did not depend on the candidate’s physical presence.

The coalition’s components were related, but they were not interchangeable. Evangelical voters formed one important source of support, and Bolsonaro’s opposition to abortion and same-sex marriage gave many a clear reason to prefer him. Religious leaders could help make political choices visible within congregations, but evangelical voters were not a uniform electorate. Their concerns included family policy and religious liberty, while their judgments about economic policy, poverty, and democratic conduct could differ. The campaign’s religious language opened a door; it did not determine every vote that crossed it.

Security constituencies responded to a different promise. Police officers, military personnel, and voters anxious about crime could value Bolsonaro’s pledge to expand gun access and give law enforcement greater freedom. His own military background reinforced that appeal. Yet the category included people with varied views of policing, the armed forces, and the proper limits of state power. A voter who wanted more effective protection did not necessarily endorse every proposal made in the name of security.

Business interests had another basis for support. Guedes’s presence and the promise of privatization suggested a government more favorable to markets and less committed to state-led economic management. For investors and business leaders, this could outweigh discomfort with Bolsonaro’s social rhetoric or his confrontational style. But business was not a single constituency, and support for economic liberalization did not mean every firm or executive agreed on the pace and scope of reform.

Anti-Workers’ Party voters were the broadest and least programmatically specific group. Some opposed the party because of corruption scandals; others rejected its economic record or its social and political agenda. Still others treated the election as a choice between two camps and voted against the Workers’ Party without strong attachment to Bolsonaro. Their negative preference could help create a majority, but it could not tell a president what those voters would support once the common opponent disappeared.

These groups overlapped. An evangelical voter might also be a police officer; a business owner might be motivated chiefly by opposition to the Workers’ Party. Their overlap helped the campaign present a coherent public image, but the reasons for support remained plural. The coalition was strongest as an electoral alliance, where a vote for one candidate could express several different judgments at once. Its unity was less certain as a governing mandate, where those judgments would have to be translated into choices among competing policies.

The case for calling Bolsonaro’s victory a coherent popular mandate deserves to be stated plainly. He finished first in the initial round and won the runoff by a clear margin. He campaigned openly on public security, economic liberalization, social conservatism, and opposition to the Workers’ Party. Voters had access to his public statements and knew that he rejected the political style of the established parties. A democratic result cannot be dismissed because the winning coalition contained different kinds of voters. If a candidate wins under the rules, he has a legitimate claim to govern.

That claim is strongest when it refers to the authority to take office and pursue the commitments made in the campaign. It is weaker when expanded into an assertion that the electorate endorsed every proposal, or that one interpretation of the victory can speak for all supporters. The official result counts votes for candidates, not reasons for voting. It cannot tell us whether a person chose Bolsonaro because of guns, family policy, privatization, anti-corruption, or opposition to the Workers’ Party. Nor does a winning margin turn a campaign promise into a detailed public instruction on how to implement it.

The formal platform makes the difficulty visible. *O Caminho da Prosperidade* offered broad directions, while campaign statements sometimes made those directions more forceful and specific. Voters could support the promise of order without endorsing every measure proposed in its name. They could favor economic reform without agreeing that every state company should be privatized. They could reject the Workers’ Party without treating Bolsonaro’s personal claims as proof of incorruptibility. Electoral support joined these positions for the purpose of choosing a president; it did not erase their differences.

The mandate argument also risks confusing popularity with administrative consent. A president may claim authority from a majority and still face a Congress elected on its own terms, courts charged with enforcing constitutional limits, and state governments with responsibilities of their own. The campaign’s anti-establishment language could make such constraints appear to supporters as obstruction, but the election did not abolish them. Winning office gives a president power to govern within the constitutional system, not a blank authorization to redefine its boundaries.

The fairest judgment is therefore neither that the victory meant nothing beyond a temporary protest nor that it expressed a single national program. Bolsonaro’s win was a genuine democratic mandate to hold the presidency and pursue the broad direction he had advertised. It was not evidence that every voter shared his priorities, accepted every campaign statement, or consented in advance to every governing choice. The distinction is especially important because his coalition had been assembled through messages that were complementary in an election but potentially in tension in office.

The official runoff returns make the scale of the victory concrete while also showing its geography. The TSE counted 57,797,847 votes for Jair Bolsonaro and 47,040,906 for Fernando Haddad on October 28, 2018. Bolsonaro carried the national contest, but the distribution was not uniform: Haddad’s strongest support lay in much of the Northeast, while Bolsonaro prevailed across much of the South, Southeast, and Center-West. The figure presents the national totals alongside selected regional shares, so the margin can be read against the map of the electorate rather than as a single undifferentiated number.

[Figure: 2018 presidential runoff: votes and regional vote shares]

The figure’s national totals describe a decisive result, while its regional shares resist the idea of a single, evenly distributed political conversion. Bolsonaro’s support was broad enough to win, but it was stronger in some regions than others, and the pattern reflected differences in political histories, economic interests, and local alignments.

That is why the result should be read as both a mandate and a coalition. The returns tell us who prevailed and by how much; they do not settle what each voter intended.
