Paulo Guedes arrived at the Economy Ministry with a program larger than any single bill. He wanted Brazil to spend less through the state, sell or open more public assets to private capital, and make investment—not public borrowing—the engine of growth. Fiscal restraint, liberalization, and investment were presented as parts of one design: a government that reduced its own claims on resources would make room for businesses to expand, while rules made simpler and markets more open would draw in capital from abroad. The design gave Bolsonaro’s government an economic identity distinct from the political rupture that had brought it to power. It also offered a way to address a persistent problem in Brazilian public finance: mandatory spending, especially pensions, left the federal government with limited room to choose where money went.

Guedes had been appointed to lead a super-ministry joining the functions of finance, planning, and trade. The consolidation signaled that economic policy would be coordinated around his priorities, though a large portfolio could not itself guarantee that the president, Congress, and the state-owned companies would follow them. Guedes’s phrase for the approach was expansionary fiscal contraction: reducing public spending, he argued, could improve confidence and encourage private investment enough to support growth. The argument was not simply that austerity was desirable. It was that restraint could produce expansion.

That promise depended on a chain of effects. Lower expected deficits might reduce uncertainty about public debt; greater confidence could encourage investment; new investment could raise productivity and employment. But each link depended on decisions by actors beyond the Economy Ministry. Businesses would invest if they expected demand and stable rules, not merely because the government announced restraint. Congress would have to approve reforms. The president would have to sustain them politically. And the distribution of the costs of adjustment would shape whether the program retained public support.

Pension reform was the clearest test of the fiscal premise. Spending on retirement and survivor benefits consumed a large share of the federal budget, and an aging population made the existing rules increasingly difficult to sustain. Guedes’s team argued that changing eligibility and benefit formulas would slow the growth of expenditure, reassure creditors, and free resources for other purposes. The reform did pass, and its scale made it a genuine achievement. Yet the government’s stated program extended well beyond pensions. Privatization of Petrobras, Eletrobras, and public banks was discussed as part of a broad transfer of economic activity to private hands. Deregulation and a simplified tax system were supposed to make Brazil more competitive. Trade agreements and a renewed investment agenda were meant to connect domestic production more closely to international markets.

The ambition was coherent; delivery was not uniform. Bolsonaro and members of the military wing of his government regarded some state companies as matters of national security, limiting the reach of the privatization program. Political bargaining in Congress narrowed proposals. The pandemic then redirected attention and public money toward emergency measures, while the government’s own choices sometimes sat uneasily beside its declared fiscal discipline. A program built around predictable rules and investor confidence also had to contend with a president whose public conflicts could make policy continuity harder to judge.

The distinction between an announced aim and an achieved result is especially important because the economic program was often treated as a single package. Pension reform became evidence that the package could work; incomplete privatization or delayed tax reform became evidence that it had not. Neither conclusion captures the variation. The government secured a consequential change to retirement rules, but it did not enact the full liberalizing agenda Guedes had described. Nor can the reform’s projected fiscal savings be counted as money already saved during Bolsonaro’s term. They were estimates of a future path, dependent on economic growth, employment, wages, and compliance with the new rules.

For supporters, the agenda offered a credible break from an expanding state and a path toward fiscal stability. For critics, it placed too much faith in private investment and too little weight on the social costs of adjustment. Both arguments concern more than ideology. They ask whether the state could reduce its future obligations without weakening the conditions that make growth broadly beneficial. The pension vote supplied a partial answer: a government with a broad, contested program could still win a major reform through Congress. It did not show that the rest of the program would follow, or that the promised expansion would arrive on schedule.

Congressional approval required a different kind of political work from the launch of Guedes’s agenda. The pension proposal had to move through a constitutional process, where the government needed supermajorities in both houses and could not rely on a simple coalition of ordinary votes. Rodrigo Maia, president of the Chamber of Deputies, became central to the path. His role was not to endorse every element of the government’s program; it was to manage the chamber’s consideration of a measure whose passage depended on legislators assembling a large majority.

The proposal began as a government bill and was examined by a special committee in the Chamber. Deputies debated its provisions, amended the text, and sent it to the floor. Because the change required a constitutional amendment, each round of voting demanded three-fifths support. The Chamber approved the proposal in two rounds in July 2019, after which the Senate considered it. Senators also made changes, and provisions altered there required renewed consideration by the Chamber. Negotiation was therefore not a single bargain but a sequence: committee review, floor votes, Senate revision, and final approval of the text that could be promulgated.

On October 22, 2019, the Senate completed the final vote on Constitutional Amendment No. 103. The vote marked the end of a legislative process that had begun months earlier and depended on congressional leaders maintaining the measure’s place on the agenda. Maia’s management of the Chamber mattered because the government did not command a disciplined majority simply by virtue of holding the presidency. Leaders in both houses had to schedule debate, negotiate changes, and keep enough legislators aligned through repeated votes.

The final amendment was narrower than the original proposal. Congress removed or altered provisions that had proved difficult to sustain, including parts that would have extended the same rules to state and municipal employees. The resulting reform changed federal retirement rules while leaving other levels of government to pursue their own changes. That limitation was not a technical footnote. It reflected the federal structure of Brazil and the political cost of imposing one settlement across governments with different fiscal conditions and constituencies.

Bolsonaro’s administration could reasonably claim the reform as a major legislative victory. Guedes supplied the policy priority, but congressional approval depended on Maia, Senate leaders, committee work, and legislators who accepted a compromise rather than the government’s original design. The path also demonstrated why presidential popularity and governing capacity are not interchangeable. A president may have a substantial electoral mandate and still need other political actors to turn a proposal into law. In this case, the reform advanced because congressional leaders made room for negotiation and because the measure’s fiscal case persuaded a broad enough majority.

What Congress approved was not an immediate reduction in pension payments. It was a change in the rules governing future eligibility and benefits, intended to slow the growth of spending over time. That distinction sits at the center of the fiscal arithmetic. The government’s projections compared an estimated path of expenditure under the old rules with a path under the new ones. The difference between those paths was described as savings. It depended on assumptions about how many people would retire, when they would qualify, how wages and contributions would change, and how the economy would perform.

The amendment raised minimum retirement ages for many workers, altered contribution requirements, and changed benefit calculations. It also introduced transition rules for people already close to retirement, so that the adjustment would not fall identically on every worker. For some, the new age threshold delayed eligibility; for others, a points system or a contribution-based transition offered a different route. The benefit formula generally tied the value of retirement more closely to a worker’s contribution history, while minimum benefits and special rules limited how far the change could reduce payments for particular groups.

Those provisions generated fiscal effects through several steps. Later retirement could mean fewer years receiving benefits and more years contributing. A longer contribution record could raise revenue. A less generous formula could reduce average benefit growth. But the projected savings were not a fixed sum waiting to be transferred into another budget line. They accumulated gradually, and the estimate depended on the number of workers formally employed and contributing. If unemployment remained high, if wages stagnated, or if informal work expanded, contributions could fall short of the assumptions built into the projection.

The figure shows how legal changes become fiscal estimates and why the same rules distribute costs differently among workers. It separates the amendment’s provisions from the assumptions needed to turn them into a projection.

[Figure: From pension rules to fiscal and distributional effects]

The distributional effects were uneven even when the fiscal objective was shared. Workers with stable formal employment were more likely to accumulate the contributions required under the new rules. People whose work histories included unemployment, informal jobs, or interrupted contributions could face a longer path to eligibility. Transition provisions softened the change for some, but no single rule could make the reform’s burden equal across occupations and life histories. Women and men also faced different age thresholds, while rural workers and people in special categories were treated under distinct rules.

The Instituição Fiscal Independente examined the projected impact and emphasized the difference between a long-term estimate and a realized result. The government’s estimate depended on a baseline: what spending would have been if the old rules had continued. Change the assumptions about growth, wages, inflation, or labor-market participation, and the estimated gap changes. The amendment could still improve the fiscal outlook without producing the exact savings first projected. Conversely, a favorable fiscal result in a later year could not be assigned to the amendment alone, since revenue and spending also respond to the economy and to other policy decisions.

This is why the reform’s achievement should be described precisely. It changed the future trajectory of pension obligations and made a large constitutional adjustment possible. It did not immediately solve Brazil’s fiscal problem, guarantee investment, or establish that the costs were distributed fairly. The law supplied a durable rule change; the savings remained a projection whose realization depended on conditions the amendment could influence only in part.

The rest of Guedes’s economic program can be sorted by what was proposed, what became law, and what was actually implemented. The categories overlap, but they prevent an announcement from being mistaken for a result.

Privatization belonged mainly to the proposal column. Guedes advocated selling major state-owned companies, including Petrobras, Eletrobras, and public banks. The ambition was to reduce the state’s direct role in production and raise proceeds that could support fiscal adjustment. Yet selling a company required legislation, valuation, political agreement, and a decision about strategic control. Bolsonaro’s government did not privatize Petrobras or Banco do Brasil. Eletrobras was privatized in 2022 through a share offering that reduced the federal government’s control, though the state retained a special voting right. The distance between the original ambition and the final transaction was substantial.

Regulatory change produced a more mixed record. The Economic Freedom Law of 2019 sought to reduce licensing requirements for low-risk activities and limit government interference in business operations. The government also advanced measures intended to improve the business environment and open parts of the economy to private participation. These changes were enacted, but their practical effects depended on implementation by agencies and local governments. A national law could simplify a rule without ensuring that every office changed its procedures at the same pace.

Infrastructure concessions and public-private partnerships moved further toward implementation in selected areas. The government continued auctions and concessions in transport and other sectors, inviting private operators to invest under contractual terms. Such projects were not equivalent to selling the state’s largest companies, but they fitted the broader effort to attract private capital to services and infrastructure. Their results varied by sector and by the terms of each contract.

Tax reform remained unfinished. Guedes’s ministry promoted simplification, including proposals to consolidate taxes, but the government did not secure a comprehensive reform during Bolsonaro’s term. Administrative reform likewise remained a proposal rather than a completed restructuring of the federal civil service. Trade policy and investment promotion continued, but they did not produce a wholesale opening of the economy. The pandemic consumed legislative attention in 2020, while disputes within the governing coalition and resistance in Congress limited the space for other measures.

The pandemic made the difference between a fiscal program and an emergency response especially visible. In 2020, the federal government and Congress created emergency cash assistance for people whose incomes were threatened by restrictions and the collapse in economic activity. Law No. 13,982, promulgated by Bolsonaro, set a monthly payment of R$600 for eligible workers for an initial period of three months. The law specified that a recipient had to be over eighteen and meet additional conditions. The payment was later extended and altered, but the original amount became the defining scale of the first phase.

The legal text is direct about the measure’s purpose and limits. It did not promise to replace a wage or insure every household against the shock. It established a transfer for people who met eligibility rules, including informal workers and other groups whose livelihoods were disrupted. The distinction between the statutory amount and the amount ultimately received by a household matters: eligibility, registration, and administrative processing determined access, while household size and other income shaped the effect of the transfer.

The R$600 payment was consequential because it arrived when millions of workers had lost earnings or could not continue their usual work. Congress pressed for a larger benefit than the lower amount initially favored by the executive, and the final payment reflected that legislative intervention as well as the government’s implementation. The program reached tens of millions of people. It also required a rapid system for identifying applicants, checking eligibility, and distributing funds through federal channels. Administrative difficulties and delays left some eligible people waiting, while fraud and mistaken payments required later review.

Household-income data from PNAD COVID19 show why the assistance cannot be treated as the sole explanation for economic outcomes. During 2020, the survey tracked employment, income, and receipt of emergency aid under exceptional conditions. The transfers helped sustain household resources, particularly among people whose labor income had fallen. At the same time, the survey captured a labor market in which jobs disappeared, hours were reduced, and informal work was disrupted. A household’s reported income could reflect the transfer, earnings from work, pensions, other benefits, and the number of people sharing resources.

The assistance therefore complicates any simple account of the government’s economic performance. It was a major federal intervention, and its scale softened the immediate loss of income for many households. It also increased public spending sharply during the crisis, while the pandemic itself reduced output and tax receipts. The fiscal expansion was not consistent with the pre-pandemic emphasis on restraint, but the emergency was not an ordinary test of that agenda. A government can be judged for the design and administration of relief without pretending that refusing relief would have preserved the original fiscal plan or protected household incomes.

The economic record from 2019 to 2022 is best read by comparing indicators rather than searching for one verdict in a single year. Brazil’s gross domestic product grew modestly in 2019, contracted sharply in 2020, rebounded in 2021, and expanded again in 2022. The sequence matters. The contraction came during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, when activity fell across the world; the subsequent growth reflected reopening, fiscal support, and recovery from a depressed base, as well as domestic production and consumption.

The 2020 decline was severe but not unique to Brazil. Lockdowns and voluntary distancing interrupted services, supply chains, and employment. The government’s emergency assistance supported household spending, while public health restrictions and fear of infection constrained activity. In 2021 and 2022, global demand recovered, commodity prices rose, and Brazil benefited from exports of agricultural and mineral goods. Those conditions aided growth, but they also fed into costs and inflation. A favorable export environment could lift national output without distributing gains evenly among workers or regions.

Inflation became a central burden. Consumer prices rose strongly in 2021 and remained high in 2022, with fuel, food, and electricity contributing to household pressure. The pandemic disrupted supply and demand; global energy and food markets tightened; drought affected electricity generation and agricultural conditions; and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 intensified international price shocks. Domestic choices also mattered. Fuel pricing, tax changes, public spending, and the timing of policy responses shaped how external pressures reached Brazilian consumers. The causes were multiple, but the political consequences were immediate: inflation reduced purchasing power and made headline growth less reassuring.

The Central Bank raised interest rates sharply, moving from historically low levels during the pandemic toward a restrictive monetary stance by 2022. Higher rates were intended to contain inflation expectations, but they also made credit more expensive and could restrain investment and consumption. The central bank’s independence, established by law in 2021, placed monetary decisions at some distance from the president’s direct control, though Bolsonaro publicly criticized interest-rate policy. The episode illustrates a division of responsibility: the president could influence fiscal choices and public debate, but he did not set the policy rate alone.

Labor-market indicators tell another part of the story. Unemployment rose during the pandemic and later declined as activity recovered. By the end of the term, the rate was lower than at its peak, but the improvement did not mean that every worker had returned to secure employment. Informality remained extensive, and many people faced low earnings or unstable work. The number of employed people could rise while job quality and household purchasing power remained weak. A falling unemployment rate is a meaningful achievement in the recovery, not a complete measure of economic security.

The comparison across years resists two easy claims. The rebound cannot be credited wholly to the administration, since global recovery, commodity prices, and the reopening of services were powerful forces. Nor can the contraction be assigned wholly to presidential policy, since the pandemic was an extraordinary shock affecting economies worldwide. Yet the government still made choices about relief, public health, fiscal support, and the consistency of its economic signals. Those choices shaped how the shock was absorbed and how quickly confidence could return.

Supporters of Guedes’s program have a serious case. Brazil entered the period with high public debt, rigid spending, and pension rules that threatened to consume an increasing share of the budget. The 2019 reform changed those rules through a difficult constitutional process. The government also enacted measures to reduce regulatory burdens, pursued concessions, and completed Eletrobras’s privatization in a limited form. Emergency assistance, despite its cost, helped sustain incomes during the pandemic. By 2022, the economy was growing and unemployment was falling. A supporter can reasonably argue that the administration accomplished more than its critics admit, especially given the pandemic and the need to negotiate with Congress.

That case is strongest when it distinguishes durable reform from short-term indicators. Pension reform was not a slogan; it altered eligibility and benefit rules. The Economic Freedom Law was not merely a campaign promise; it changed the legal environment for some businesses. The recovery in employment was not imaginary. And the emergency transfer was not a minor program. These achievements deserve recognition even if they do not validate every part of Guedes’s theory or prove that the government’s policies caused the subsequent growth.

The limits appear when the program is judged by its own breadth. Privatization of the largest state companies remained incomplete, comprehensive tax reform did not pass, and administrative reform stalled. The government’s fiscal language also shifted under pressure. Emergency spending was necessary to respond to the pandemic, but later measures and political demands continued to test the commitment to restraint. The spending cap, already under strain, became a site of repeated negotiation rather than a stable anchor. Investors looking for predictable rules had to assess not only the Economy Ministry’s plans but also presidential choices and congressional bargains.

Distribution further complicates the supporter’s account. A reform that reduces long-term pension spending can improve the fiscal outlook while imposing greater difficulty on workers with interrupted or informal employment. A simpler regulatory environment may help firms without guaranteeing that gains reach households. Growth in aggregate output can coexist with high food prices and insecure work. These are not reasons to dismiss reform; they are reasons to ask who bears its costs and who receives its benefits.

Critics, in turn, can overstate the case if they treat every disappointing outcome as proof that the program was empty. The pension amendment was consequential, and the economic shock of 2020 cannot be used as a neutral baseline against which the government’s entire record is measured. But the administration’s uneven delivery was not only a consequence of external events. Bolsonaro’s own political priorities, resistance to some privatizations, and conflict with other actors affected the space for coordinated economic policy. Guedes’s formal authority did not make him the sole author of what the government did.

In 2018, Bolsonaro’s registered program offered broad signals: security, economic change, national sovereignty, and social conservatism. Four years later, his reelection plan, filed with the Superior Electoral Court, did something different. It made the presidency itself its principal evidence. Titled *For the Good of Brazil*, the document presented programs already under way as reasons to continue the government and placed the defense of its record beside the promise of a conservative agenda. The word “family” appeared sixty-seven times. Freedom occupied the opening chapter, defined through family, democracy, economic liberty, property, the right to life of the unborn, and the right to express opinions and live by one’s values.

That shift from promise to defense is useful for judging the administration on its own terms. A program written for reelection is not an audit, and its emphasis cannot show how well a policy worked. But it does reveal what Bolsonaro’s campaign chose to make central at the end of his term. The 2022 plan did not chiefly ask voters to imagine a new government. It asked them to preserve the one they had.

The official 2018 program had made room for a wide coalition. Its ambitions included economic liberalization and public security, alongside national and social themes that could speak to voters with different priorities. The later document narrowed the focus to continuity and identity. Its repeated language of freedom connected economic choice to religious and moral convictions, while its account of government emphasized programs already operating. The campaign’s argument was that these aims belonged together: a government that defended family and individual liberty could also claim credit for economic reform and public administration.

Some of that record was concrete. Congress enacted Constitutional Amendment No. 103 in 2019, changing federal retirement rules after negotiations that depended on congressional leaders as well as the administration. The Economic Freedom Law reduced licensing requirements for low-risk activities. The federal government expanded digital access to services through gov.br, and Eletrobras was privatized in 2022 through a share offering, with the state retaining a special voting right. These were consequential changes, though they did not amount to the wholesale retreat of the state that some supporters had hoped for. Banco do Brasil remained public, and the broader program of privatization and investment did not advance at the scale implied by the campaign’s economic ambitions.

The same test applies to the plan’s language of freedom. A government may defend religious conviction and property rights while also being judged by whether it protects the conditions under which citizens can exercise rights equally. In the Amazon, rising deforestation and weaker enforcement damaged the government’s claim to have balanced development with stewardship. Indigenous land protections became a site of conflict rather than a settled guarantee. The administration did not abolish environmental agencies, but its public signals and policy choices made enforcement less credible. The difference between a stated priority and a governing result was visible in the distance between the language of sovereignty and the practical loss of confidence among Brazil’s partners.

The pandemic exposed a sharper gap. Bolsonaro’s government created emergency assistance, initially set at R$600 a month for eligible recipients after Congress raised the administration’s proposed amount, and supported the AstraZeneca-Fiocruz vaccine partnership. Those actions mattered to millions of people. Yet the federal response also included repeated presidential opposition to broad restrictions, conflict with governors, and consequential delays in vaccine procurement. Shared public-health responsibilities did not remove the federal government’s power to coordinate purchases or communicate risk. The 2022 program’s emphasis on continuity asked voters to treat these choices as part of a successful record, but the record was mixed by the administration’s own conduct.

The presidency’s political meaning was tested after Bolsonaro left office, when a dispute over his public conduct became a case before Brazil’s electoral court. On June 30, 2023, the Superior Electoral Court, sitting in Brasília, found him ineligible to stand for office for eight years. The case concerned his meeting with foreign ambassadors at the presidential residence on July 18, 2022, and his attacks on the reliability of Brazil’s electronic voting system.

The meeting was not a private conversation. Bolsonaro used his position as president to address ambassadors accredited to Brazil and discuss the country’s election system before the October vote. He repeated claims that electronic voting was vulnerable and cast doubt on the system’s reliability, though he did not present evidence to substantiate the allegations. Public television broadcast the event, and it circulated widely. Its setting mattered: foreign representatives were being asked to hear a president challenge the machinery through which his own mandate would be renewed.

The TSE’s case proceeded under electoral law, not as a general judgment on Bolsonaro’s politics. The court considered whether the meeting and the use of presidential communication had abused political power and the means of communication, giving Bolsonaro an unfair advantage and damaging the equality of the contest. It did not need to prove that any vote had been altered. The question was the conduct of a candidate who was also the sitting president, the reach of the event, and its capacity to distort the conditions of the election.

Benedito Gonçalves, the rapporteur, presented the case to the court. The majority concluded that Bolsonaro had used the authority and visibility of his office to spread unsupported attacks on the voting system in a setting that magnified their effect. The court found him responsible for abuse of political power and misuse of the media, and imposed ineligibility for eight years, counted from the 2022 election. The ruling did not remove him from office retroactively, overturn the election result, or declare that his supporters had committed wrongdoing merely by believing his claims.

Electoral law protects more than the accuracy of a count after voting has ended; it also protects the fairness of the contest while voters are deciding. A president has access to official platforms and public attention unavailable to an ordinary candidate. When he uses those advantages to undermine confidence in the electoral process without substantiation, the issue is not simply whether voters were persuaded. It is whether the contest was conducted on equal terms and whether public power was used for a candidate’s benefit.

The ruling was not the last word in every legal matter involving Bolsonaro, and its sanction did not settle the broader political dispute. The June 2023 decision nevertheless established a specific legal finding about a specific event: Bolsonaro’s meeting with ambassadors and his attacks on the voting system violated electoral rules in a way that justified a period of ineligibility. That finding concerns the conduct and sanction in this case; it does not amount to a complete account of his presidency.

Bolsonaro and his supporters treated the decision as political persecution, arguing that the court had punished a leader for raising questions about election security. Their argument draws force from a real democratic principle: public officials and candidates may scrutinize electoral procedures, and courts should not convert criticism into an offense merely because it is unwelcome. Brazil’s voting system is not beyond question simply because it is electronic, and public confidence cannot be commanded by decree.

But the TSE’s finding was not that any criticism of electronic voting was unlawful. The case concerned the president’s use of a formal meeting with foreign ambassadors to repeat claims without evidence, in the months before an election in which he was a candidate. The legal question was whether that conduct abused his office and the communication advantages attached to it. The political claim of persecution addresses the legitimacy of the court and the meaning of the sanction; it does not erase the conduct the court examined.

Nor does the legal ruling prove every broader criticism made of Bolsonaro. It does not establish that every supporter was hostile to democracy, or that every political appeal to distrust was criminal. It identifies a narrower responsibility: a sitting president used a high-profile official event to attack the voting system and was found to have violated electoral law. A political leader may call the decision unjust; that response remains part of political debate.

The two kinds of judgment answer different questions. The TSE determined whether the conduct met the legal standard for abuse and what sanction followed. Supporters’ arguments ask whether the court’s decision was fair, whether scrutiny of elections is being chilled, and whether the sanction will exclude a popular figure from political competition. Those questions deserve consideration, but they cannot substitute for the court’s findings about the event. Conversely, the legal judgment cannot by itself settle the quality of Bolsonaro’s whole presidency.

His political reach remained measurable, though not in a way that can be reduced to a single vote total. In October 2024, Brazilians elected mayors and municipal councillors across the country. The results showed that conservative and right-wing parties remained powerful, while individual candidates’ performance varied from city to city. Bolsonaro endorsed candidates in several contests; some won and others lost. A vote for an endorsed mayoral candidate, however, is not a direct ballot for Bolsonaro. Local contests turn on municipal services, alliances, party organization, and the standing of the candidate as well as national politics.

The first round gave the Liberal Party, Bolsonaro’s party, a strong position in many municipalities and made it one of the leading forces in the mayoral contests. In São Paulo, Bolsonaro backed Ricardo Nunes, the incumbent, who advanced to the runoff and won. The result showed the value of Bolsonaro’s endorsement when attached to a candidate with an existing municipal coalition and a broad base of support. Nunes had his own record, allies, and reasons for attracting votes.

Other contests made the limits clearer. In some cities, Bolsonaro’s preferred candidate failed to advance or lost, despite the national attention attached to the endorsement. Municipal elections reward organization that can reach voters repeatedly and assemble local alliances; a national figure can help mobilize supporters, but may also make a race more polarizing. The outcome depends on the candidate and the city.

The results also cannot be read as a direct measure of the 2022 presidential electorate. Voters choose a mayor to manage local services and a president to lead the country; turnout and candidate selection differ. Party success can reflect a coalition’s strength without proving personal loyalty to its most prominent figure. Bolsonaro remained an influential endorser, but the 2024 results did not confer on him an independent mandate, nor did they test him as a candidate.

They did show that his political network had not disappeared after the election loss and the TSE ruling. The Liberal Party, allied conservative parties, and local candidates could still draw on the constituency that had supported him. His influence was real but mediated: it operated through endorsements, party ties, and the continued appeal of a political identity, rather than through a direct national vote in 2024. That distinction matters when assessing both the durability of his movement and the limits imposed by his legal status.

The strongest case made by Bolsonaro’s supporters begins with representation. For years, many voters felt that the political class treated their moral views, concerns about crime, and distrust of the Workers’ Party as backward or illegitimate. Bolsonaro spoke in a language that did not ask them to soften those convictions before entering public life. He made conservative Christians, security-minded voters, and people hostile to the established left feel that their preferences could shape national policy. This was not an illusion created by one man alone; it reflected a durable coalition and a genuine demand for political recognition.

Supporters can also point to changes that were more than symbolic. Pension reform altered the federal system, the Economic Freedom Law reduced some barriers for low-risk businesses, and digital services expanded. Eletrobras’s privatization changed the ownership structure of a major state-controlled company. The administration’s emergency assistance reached eligible households during the economic shock of the pandemic, while the AstraZeneca-Fiocruz partnership contributed to vaccine supply. These measures were not all designed or passed by Bolsonaro personally, but they occurred under his government and form part of its record.

Yet representation cannot be the only measure of a presidency. A president who gives neglected voters a voice remains responsible for how he uses the office and what his administration accomplishes. The pension reform required sustained congressional work, and its passage depended on legislators who were not merely extensions of the president. By contrast, the broader promises of privatization and investment were unevenly delivered. The government’s environmental record weakened enforcement while deforestation rose. During COVID-19, emergency aid and vaccine support coexisted with public resistance to restrictions and delays in procurement. These are not minor qualifications to a record of success; they are part of its substance.

Nor does the argument from representation excuse attacks on the electoral system. A leader may question procedures and demand answers, but a president’s unsupported claims carry a weight that ordinary criticism does not. The TSE ruling addressed a particular use of presidential power, not the beliefs of millions of voters. This distinction allows supporters’ grievances to be heard without treating every legal finding as partisan punishment, and it allows criticism of Bolsonaro without denying that his constituency had legitimate political demands.

The supporter case is strongest when it insists that voters chose a real program and that the administration enacted consequential reforms. It is weakest when it treats popular identification as proof of administrative success or institutional innocence. The same presidency could represent people who had felt excluded, pass important economic measures, and still fail to coordinate effectively in a national emergency or protect confidence in democratic procedures. Recognition is a political achievement; it is not a substitute for governing.

Political appeal and administrative effectiveness are related, but they are not interchangeable. Bolsonaro’s appeal rested partly on his ability to speak directly to voters who believed conventional politics had ignored them. His plain, combative language made conflict itself seem like evidence of authenticity. He could present a dispute with judges, journalists, governors, or international critics as a contest between ordinary citizens and powerful interests. That style strengthened identification. It did not necessarily help the government carry policy through.

The pension reform illustrates the difference. Its passage required negotiation with Congress, especially with Rodrigo Maia and other legislators who could assemble votes. The reform was consequential, but its success depended on bargaining and legislative work that did not arise from presidential confrontation alone. Bolsonaro could claim the result as part of his administration’s record; he could not plausibly treat it as proof that personal conflict was an effective substitute for coalition-building.

The pandemic showed the costs more starkly. Brazil’s public-health system distributed responsibilities among the Union, states, and municipalities, and the Supreme Federal Court affirmed that local governments could act within their powers. That division did not leave the federal government powerless. The Ministry of Health negotiated national purchases, and the federal government could coordinate information and procurement. Bolsonaro’s public opposition to broad restrictions, his conflicts with governors, and delays in accepting early Pfizer offers weakened the coherence of the national response. Emergency aid and vaccine partnerships were real achievements, but they do not erase the consequences of those choices.

Administrative effectiveness also requires attention to continuity. Frequent changes among senior officials and public disputes over policy made it harder to maintain a stable direction, even where capable officials and agencies continued their work. The environmental record showed how a government could retain formal agencies while diminishing the credibility of enforcement. The question is not whether Bolsonaro had a popular mandate or whether some policies succeeded, but whether his administration could convert political support into sustained, coordinated results.

Bolsonaro’s public conduct repeatedly favoured immediacy: direct messages, public challenges, and sharp divisions between allies and opponents. That approach could keep supporters engaged and force neglected issues into debate. It also made cooperation more difficult when success depended on trust among the presidency, Congress, courts, state governments, and technical agencies. The result was not failure everywhere. His achievements were clearest where institutions and legislators could carry work forward; his weaknesses grew more consequential when coordination and credible communication were essential.

The unresolved question is how far those observable habits explain the unevenness. Bolsonaro could accept congressional bargaining when a major reform required it, yet often treated other disagreements as public contests in which compromise risked appearing as surrender. That pattern is visible in the record; a private motive is not needed to describe it. Does it reflect a durable limit on his ability to build coalitions, or a political method that succeeds when supporters reward confrontation and fails when government requires continuity across institutions?

The question reaches beyond one administration because the coalition Bolsonaro assembled did not vanish with his defeat. Conservative parties retained local strength, candidates continued to seek his endorsement, and his public voice remained influential even after the TSE judgment. At the same time, the 2024 municipal results showed that influence had to pass through local candidates and alliances. A national leader could help define a contest without controlling its outcome.

His political future also depends on legal proceedings and the choices of other politicians. The eight-year ineligibility ruling sharply constrained his ability to run for office under its terms, while leaving open the possibility that his supporters could organize around other candidates. Whether those candidates can hold together a coalition spanning religious conservatives, security voters, business interests, and anti-left voters is not settled by Bolsonaro’s continuing popularity, or by the fact that some of his preferred candidates won municipal office.

A portrait of his influence must therefore include both presence and dependence. Bolsonaro remains a recognizable national figure whose endorsements can matter, but his political reach is mediated by party leaders, local candidates, and voters who may share some of his priorities without accepting every position he takes. The 2024 contests demonstrated that his movement could compete without converting every race into a personal referendum. They also showed that local organization and candidate credibility could matter more than a presidential endorsement.

His influence may endure as a movement, a set of policy commitments, and a language of opposition. Whether it endures as a governing project depends on what its leaders do when they must bargain, administer, and accept constraints. The judgment of Bolsonaro’s presidency is therefore not that popularity was false or achievement absent. Representation and reform were real; the costs of confrontation became clearest when Brazil needed a president to coordinate the country and sustain confidence in its rules.
